10	## Discussions this session that are NOT in any plan (2026-08-19 → 21)
11	
12	Recorded here because git cannot tell you any of it, and the user asked for a clean context.
13	
14	### ⚠️ Redis — asked, and the answer is NO
15	
16	*"Maybe change to redis (idk for what, maybe caching)"*. Everything Redis would front is already cached
17	closer to the data: the day's looks in Postgres (Decision 5 IS the cache), weather via
18	`fetch(…, {revalidate:1800})` per rounded coordinate, signed URLs in `lib/storage/signed.ts`, sessions
19	in Supabase Auth cookies, the reroll quota in `generation_events`. Adding it means a second cache in
20	front of things that are already fast, plus a service to run, pay for and secure — against Decision 4.
21	
22	**The ONE place it could earn its keep, later:** `use cache` defaults to in-memory, so its entries die
23	with the serverless instance. Durable `use cache` wants `use cache: remote` or a `cacheHandlers` entry,
24	and that is where an Upstash/Redis would plug in. That is the RENDERING cache, not the data.
25	
26	### ⚠️ Microservices — asked, and the answer is NO, and it is not close
27	
28	The honest trigger for microservices is organisational: many teams deploying independently. This is one
29	person. Splitting it trades a codebase you can hold in your head for network calls, version skew and
30	four deploy pipelines, to serve a handful of Server Actions. A monolith is still right at 100× current
31	users. The parts that could have been services already are not — background removal is client-side
32	(Decision 2), and scheduled work would be `pg_cron`.
33	
34	### Next.js 16.3 upgrade — done, PR #39
35	
36	⚠️ **`npm install` failed three times with `ENOTEMPTY`** before it worked: macOS seeds `.DS_Store` into
37	`node_modules`, and npm's rename-to-staging then cannot clear the directory. Fix:
38	`find node_modules -name .DS_Store -delete` plus removing stale `.<pkg>-XXXXXXXX` staging dirs at any
39	depth. The same family as the iCloud `" 2."` duplicates that break `tsc`, and it recurred in `.next`
40	later in the session.
41	
42	⚠️ **`AGENTS.md` is gitignored** — `next dev` writes and maintains it from 16.3, and meta/authorship
43	docs stay out of git here.
44	
45	### The e2e decision, and why it changed the whole session
46	
47	*"i want playwright with e2e tests, unit tests are not so good."* The record backed it: sorting every
48	defect of the previous week by what caught it, **every user-visible one** was found by real data on a
49	real screen. ⚠️ **But be precise about what e2e fixes** — it would have caught "1 coats" and
50	"Adds 1%"; it would NOT have caught "258 is uncredible" (a judgement call) or "outerwear is
51	unreachable" (found by a probe sweeping the closet across temperatures). **The measurement probes stay.**
52	
53	CI decisions: **the Haiku call is stubbed** (`FITCHECK_STUB_AI`, inside `rerank()` so the shipped path
54	is the tested path), and **Supabase runs in the workflow**, migrating to a hosted project later.

58	1. ⚠️ **Open-Meteo is not licensed for commercial use**, and after this week's weather work it is the
59	   backbone of the generator. It is the only item that can stop a launch. It is a DECISION (licence or
60	   swap provider), not engineering.
61	2. **Packing mode is advertised in the upgrade sheet and does not exist.** Build it or cut the copy

63	3. **13 stale branches** (verified merged) still un-deleted.

65	## Merged (PRs #42–#45) — Instant Navigations, and what it actually taught
66	
67	All 12 routes are `◐` partial-prerender. `npm run insights` and `instant()` are the guards.
68	
69	### ⚠️ The security worry answered itself — by the framework
70	
71	The plan treated the auth boundary as the dangerous part. **Next refuses at build time**: writing a
72	`use cache` function that reads `cookies()` fails with *"Accessing Dynamic data sources inside a cache
73	scope is not supported."* The session cannot reach a cached fragment at all, so per-user data can only
74	be cached by passing the user id as an ARGUMENT — which puts it in the key. Stronger than the
75	convention the plan relied on.
76	
77	### ⚠️ Three defects, and none of them showed up in `npm run build`
78	
79	1. **Sheets stopped closing.** Routes are preserved with React `<Activity hidden>` now, not unmounted,
80	   so `useState` survives navigation — back with the Refine sheet open and it was still open on return.
81	   Cleanup effects on four sheets. ⚠️ **The test uses the BACK BUTTON, not a nav tap**: a modal backdrop
82	   covers the nav by design, so tapping a tab with a sheet open is not a path a user has.
83	2. **`blocking-prerender-current-time` on TEN routes**, from `supabase.auth.getUser()` checking token
84	   expiry against `Date.now()`. Fixed with `connection()` in the one shared factory. ⚠️ **The build was
85	   clean throughout** — only the dev overlay shows it, which is why `npm run insights` now automates
86	   the walk. ⚠️ **Scope, honestly: the shells rendered correctly either way** (byte-identical at 6553);
87	   what it fixes is 11 error-level log lines per walk. An earlier claim that every route was "de-opting"
88	   was overstated.
89	3. **Four routes had EMPTY shells** — nothing but the bottom nav. Tapping Profile showed a blank screen
90	   for 836ms. Found only by Task 6's before/after measurement, which is the step most tempting to skip.
91	   Diary went **840ms → 54ms**.
92	
93	### ⚠️ The profile is the lesson worth keeping
94	
95	Its design has **no title**, so the first shell fix invented one — it painted instantly and then
96	VANISHED when the body arrived. **New UI nobody designed is not a shell.** Its real static content is
97	the link rows.
98	
99	### Recorded deviations, not hidden
100	
101	- **Task 1 Step 1**: the plan said *"record the decision either way; do not silently hand-roll what a
102	  first-party tool does"* about Vercel's `next-cache-components-adoption` skill. **I hand-rolled it
103	  without looking.** The migration is complete, so running it now proves nothing.
104	- **Task 3 Step 4**: never read `authentication-with-cache-components`. The constraint was derived
105	  empirically instead and held.
106	- **Task 6 Step 3**: 6 of 12 shells checked against `DESIGN.md`. **Folded into queue #16**, the
107	  whole-product design audit, rather than done twice.
108	
109	## Merged (PR #41) — the e2e journeys (plan #13a, Task 2)
110	
111	12 e2e tests, ~9s locally / ~6m in CI. Closet grid → item detail → back (including a deep link with no
112	history, the PWA cold-start path PR #21 fixed), cost-per-wear absent rather than €0.00 when unpriced,
113	Wear Stats in BOTH tiers, the upgrade sheet, and the zero-wear state.
114	
115	**The assertion the file exists for: the gap card's reason must name the same slot it recommends.**
116	⚠️ **Verified negatively** (plan Task 4) — pointing the reason at the wrong slot turns it red **on the
117	reason assertion while the recommendation assertion still passes**, which is exactly the shape of the
118	2026-08-18 defect.
119	
120	- ⚠️ **The upgrade sheet is checked by CLICKING its action, not by reading a z-index.** `MobileNav` is
121	  `z-50` and renders after the page content, so it has painted over a sheet's primary action before
122	  (`RefineSheet`). A z-index assertion passes while the button is still covered; a click does not.
123	- ⚠️ **Every helper that mutates the seeded world restores it.** `workers: 1` makes that safe, but a
124	  spec leaving the tier on `free` would silently change what every later spec asserts.
125	- ⚠️ **CI caught a strict-mode violation the local run did not**: the item name renders twice on the
126	  detail screen (serif title + spec row), so a bare `getByText` matched two elements. **Locators for
127	  seeded names must be explicit about `.first()`** — the failure reads like a missing element and is
128	  not one.
129	- The `e2e` job is capped at **12 minutes**; its first failure sat for 15 before the runner gave up.
130	
131	## Merged (PR #39) — Next.js 16.3.1
132	
133	Minor bump, no application code. The wins need none: **~22% more requests under load** (App Router SSR
134	moved from web streams to native Node streams), prefetch inlining, Turbopack FS cache for builds, ~90%
135	less dev memory. ⚠️ `package.json` already allowed 16.3.x via the caret — only the lockfile held us at
136	16.2.9. ⚠️ **`AGENTS.md` is gitignored**: `next dev` writes and maintains it from 16.3, and
137	meta/authorship docs stay out of git here (same rule as `CLAUDE.md`, `DESIGN.md`, `docs/`).
138	
139	⚠️ **`npm install` failed three times with `ENOTEMPTY`** before it worked: macOS seeds `.DS_Store` into
140	`node_modules`, and npm's rename-to-staging then cannot clear the directory. Fix:
141	`find node_modules -name .DS_Store -delete` plus removing the stale `.<pkg>-XXXXXXXX` staging dirs at
142	any depth. Same family as the iCloud `" 2."` duplicates that break `tsc`.
143	
144	## Merged (PR #40) — the e2e foundation (plan #13a, Task 1)
145	
146	**User decision 2026-08-19: *"i want playwright with e2e tests, unit tests are not so good."*** The
147	record agrees — sorting every defect of the previous week by what caught it, **every user-visible one**
148	was found by real data on a real screen.
149	
150	- **WebKit on an iPhone viewport, and nothing else.** iOS Safari is the target, and a desktop width has
151	  already produced a false finding here once.
152	- **`next start`, not `next dev`** — dev disables prefetching entirely.
153	- ⚠️ **The model call is stubbed inside `rerank()`** behind `FITCHECK_STUB_AI`, **not** in a test file,
154	  so the whole deterministic pipeline still runs and the path under test is the path that ships. CI
155	  spends nothing and needs no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
156	- ⚠️ **Auth cookies are serialised BY `@supabase/ssr`**, never hand-written — the cookie is chunked and
157	  its name derived from the project URL. The magic link cannot be driven from outside the browser:
158	  `/auth/callback` is PKCE and needs a verifier only the initiating browser holds.
159	- **A dedicated seeded user** (`e2e@fitcheck.test`), so nobody ever again reassigns the developer's real
160	  `wear_logs` by hand to photograph an empty state.
161	
162	### ⚠️ Five defects found while building it — each by the suite refusing to pass
163	
164	1. `items.image_url` is `NOT NULL`.
165	2. **`outfit_items.slot` is `NOT NULL`, and the insert failed SILENTLY** because its error went
166	   unchecked — leaving `/stats` rendering a `MOST WORN` header with nothing under it. **Check every
167	   seed error**; a seed that fails quietly makes every downstream assertion vacuous while CI reads green.
168	3. **A storage path with no object behind it hangs `page.goto` until timeout**, because the image never
169	   loads. The seed uploads real 1×1 PNGs.
170	4. ⚠️ **Vitest was collecting the Playwright specs**, reporting `1 failed | 77 passed` at the FILE level
171	   while `Tests 737 passed` read green. The suite was red and looked green. `vitest.config.ts` now
172	   excludes `e2e/**`.
173	5. **The Playwright `setup` project had no device**, so it defaulted to Chromium while CI installs only
174	   WebKit — green locally, red in CI, and green locally only because Chromium happened to be installed
175	   by hand.
176	
177	**The negative test was run** (plan Task 4): the pluralisation guard was verified by reverting the
178	"Worn once" fix and confirming it goes red on `"Worn 1 times"`, then restoring it. ⚠️ **`reuseExistingServer`
179	means a stale local server can serve OLD code and pass** — kill port 3000 before any negative check.

64	### ⚠️ Settings (#9b): do NOT ship "Auto-log worn looks" as written
65	
66	The plan specifies *"when on, opening a look after 18:00 local logs it."* **Rejected — opening a look is
67	not wearing it.** `wear_logs` is the foundation of cost-per-wear, streaks, most-worn, gathering-dust and
68	gap analysis, i.e. of everything Pro sells. Logging views as wears inflates all of it permanently, with
69	no way afterwards to tell a fabricated wear from a real one — poisoning the paid feature to save one tap.
70	`MONETISATION.md` §1: *"they pay for it in month three, once the data is theirs."*
71	
72	**Build an evening confirmation instead** (agreed with the user 2026-08-05): if you opened a look today
73	and logged nothing, ask once — *"Did you wear <look> today?"* — **Yes / No**. Yes writes the same row the
74	button writes; No writes nothing and it does not ask again that day. Triggers when the app is next opened
75	after ~18:00 local, so it needs no web-push and is buildable now.
76	
77	Two details that decide whether it helps or hurts: **Yes and No must be equally easy** (a lone "Yes" with
78	a dismiss ✕ gets tapped to clear it, and the data inflates anyway), and it asks only about looks actually
79	opened, most recent first — dwell time is not tracked, so "most recent" is the honest simple choice.
80	
81	It is **bigger than a toggle**, so it wants its own small plan. Settings then ships **rain guard as its
82	only live toggle** — which is that plan's own stated rule: *"rendering a switch that schedules nothing is
83	the lie this plan is trying to avoid."*
84	
85	**Price/copy decisions already applied in #27** (kept here for the record): the price is **€5**, not the
86	design's £5 — the app targets the EU and every other price renders in euro. The feature list still ships
87	verbatim, **packing mode included**, which is deliberate while nothing can be bought; it must be built
88	before Pro is actually sold, or dropped from the copy then.

176	### The canonical screen: item detail (`Fitcheck.dc.html:587-657`)
177	
178	**User decision, 2026-07-28: "we should still follow this detail page for cloth, it's the best."** When
179	a new screen has no design of its own — a generated concept, a Pro feature, an empty state — derive it
180	from this one. It is the most complete expression of the system, and the plan that builds it is queue #5

182	
183	The reusable vocabulary, in the order the screen uses it:
184	
185	| Pattern | How it works |
186	|---|---|
187	| **Brand kicker** | Uppercase, letterspaced, muted, tiny — sits *above* the title (`HARTLEY`). Wayfinding, never content. |
188	| **Serif display title** | Libre Caslon Text, large, cream. The name of the thing (`Pale Blue Oxford`). |
189	| **Grotesk subtitle** | Hanken Grotesk, muted, `·` as the separator (`Oxford shirt · Pale blue`). |
190	| **Stat tiles** | A row of 3 rounded surfaces: serif value on top, uppercase micro-label under it (`30 / TIMES WORN`). The row is the screen's "how you actually wear it" summary. |
191	| **Labelled meter** | Uppercase kicker left, plain-language value right (`FORMALITY … Smart casual`), then 5 segments with the filled ones in rust. Never a number on its own — always the word. |
192	| **Spec table** | Hairline-divided rows, muted label left, cream value right. Multi-values joined with `·` (`Spring · Autumn · Winter`). |
193	| **Horizontal card row** | Uppercase kicker (`GOES WITH`) over a scrolling row of cutout cards with a caption under each. |
194	| **Bottom action bar** | One small secondary icon button + one full-width cream pill for the single primary action (`Style an outfit with this`). One primary action per screen. |
195	
196	Two things this screen encodes that are easy to lose: **cutouts are the hero and everything else is
197	quiet around them**, and **the rust accent appears exactly once** (the meter) — the One Rust Rule in
198	`DESIGN.md`. A concept with two rust elements is already off-system.

Measured the actual render sizes rather than trusting the number in the plan. Here's where I land.

## 1. Thumbnail `maxPx` → **480**, one derivative

The plan's number is right, and now there's a reason behind it. On a 390px iPhone viewport:

| surface | CSS box | at DPR 3 |
|---|---|---|
| **closet grid** (`columns-2`, `px-6`, `gap-3`, card `p-5`, tallest cell 200) | ~125 × 160 | **375 × 480** |
| "Goes with" row (`w-[92px]`, `p-3`) | 68 × 68 | 204 |
| diary cell | ~45 × 54 | 162 |

One surface sets the ceiling — the tallest masonry cell at 3× — and it lands on 480 almost exactly. Everything else is far under. Because the images are `object-contain`, a tall coat is height-constrained (160→480) and wide shoes are width-constrained (125→375), so **480 as max-dimension** is the correct form of the cap, not a width.

Don't add a second smaller derivative for the diary and the goes-with row. It doubles upload CPU and storage to save a few kB on surfaces that are already small, and it adds a third path to `displayPath` that every reader has to reason about.

## 2. `original.jpg` → **keep it**, and I'd go further: this decision is smaller than the plan makes it sound

The plan frames it as "73% of stored bytes," which reads alarming. But stored bytes aren't the constraint you're worried about — **egress** is, and `original.jpg` contributes essentially none of it. `displayPath` is `cutout_url ?? image_url`, so it's served only when background removal failed. It's ~271 kB × item sitting at rest: a 100-item closet is ~27 MB of storage and ~0 MB of transfer.

So: keeping it costs almost nothing on the axis that matters, and it's the only re-taggable source if you ever change the tagging schema or the cutout pipeline. Deleting it is irreversible and leaves a failed cutout permanently unrecoverable. Keep, and revisit only if storage itself ever becomes the binding cost — which it won't before egress does.

## 3. Sequencing → **start #13c now**, work Open-Meteo in parallel

Open-Meteo is the only launch blocker, but it's not engineering — it's reading a licence page or sending an email, and it needs you, not me. It doesn't gate #13c. So they run side by side rather than one behind the other.

Two smaller calls while we're here:

- **Packing mode** — leave it parked. It's correctly deliberate that the copy ships verbatim while nothing can be bought; the decision only becomes real at checkout. Revisit with #17 (Stripe), not now.
- **13 merged branches** — delete them. Verified merged just now (2 local, 11 remote); `git branch -r --no-merged main` is empty.

One flag on #13c itself before I start: **Task 5 is a backfill of the 28 existing items**, and the last backfill plan (`cutout-backfill`) died because the local storage volume was lost. Worth confirming those 28 items still have objects behind them before the plan assumes it can read and re-encode them — I'll check that in Task 0 rather than discovering it at Task 5.

# Executing Plans

## Overview

Load plan, review critically, execute all tasks, report when complete.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the executing-plans skill to implement this plan."

**Note:** Tell your human partner that Superpowers works much better with access to subagents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Codex App, Copilot CLI, and Gemini CLI all qualify; see the per-platform tool refs in `../using-superpowers/references/`). If subagents are available, use superpowers:subagent-driven-development instead of this skill.

## The Process

### Step 1: Load and Review Plan
1. Ensure an isolated workspace: use superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one
2. Read plan file
3. Review critically - identify any questions or concerns about the plan
4. If concerns: Raise them with your human partner before starting
5. If no concerns: Create todos for the plan items and proceed

### Step 2: Execute Tasks

For each task:
1. Mark as in_progress
2. Follow each step exactly (plan has bite-sized steps)
3. Run verifications as specified
4. Mark as completed

### Step 3: Complete Development

After all tasks complete and verified:
- Announce: "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch
- Follow that skill to verify tests, present options, execute choice

## When to Stop and Ask for Help

**STOP executing immediately when:**
- Hit a blocker (missing dependency, test fails, instruction unclear)
- Plan has critical gaps preventing starting
- You don't understand an instruction
- Verification fails repeatedly

**Ask for clarification rather than guessing.**

## When to Revisit Earlier Steps

**Return to Review (Step 1) when:**
- Partner updates the plan based on your feedback
- Fundamental approach needs rethinking

**Don't force through blockers** - stop and ask.

## Remember
- Review plan critically first
- Follow plan steps exactly
- Don't skip verifications
- Reference skills when plan says to
- Stop when blocked, don't guess
- Never start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent

content.text:
**#13c `image-weight` is built and verified.** Branch `feat/image-weight`, 5 commits, tree clean, not merged.

## What it does

A 480px WebP derivative generated **in the browser at upload**, from the cutout, stored as `thumb.webp` beside it. `items.thumb_url` is nullable; `displayPath(item, "thumb" | "full" = "full")` falls through to the cutout, then the original. Zero per-view cost — the same bargain as Decision 2.

| surface | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| closet grid | 493.5 kB | **97.8 kB** | −80% |
| diary month | 211.5 kB | **41.9 kB** | −80% |
| item detail | 352.5 kB | **126.4 kB** | −64% |
| stylist flat-lay | 211.5 kB | 211.5 kB | unchanged, deliberately |

Item detail's remaining 126.4 kB is precisely the hero at full quality plus four thumbnails. The flat-lay and the hero are the product and were left alone.

## Verified

757 unit tests · 27 e2e · `tsc` clean · `build` clean · `insights` clean · lint identical to main's baseline (13 problems both sides, none in files I touched). All three thumbnail surfaces screenshotted on a booted **iPhone 17 Pro simulator** with your real 26-piece closet — grid, diary and the "Goes with" tiles are all sharp, and the diary's colour recall holds at 45px.

## Three things it cost, now written into STATE.md

1. **The storage folder is not `items.id`.** `uploadAndTag` mints its own `crypto.randomUUID()` for the path while the row gets a different id from its default. My first backfill built paths from `item.id` and put all 26 thumbnails in folders holding nothing else — which still *works*, since `thumb_url` points at them, and is silently wrong. Caught it, removed the misplaced objects, re-ran from `cutout_url`.
2. **`.map(displayPath)` was point-free at all five call sites**, so the new optional `size` argument would have received the array index. `tsc` caught it; all five are explicit lambdas now.
3. **The diary measured zero images at first** — its only seeded wear is fixed at `2026-01-15` and `/calendar` renders the current month. Exactly the plan's own "measure the right thing" trap.

## Two deviations, deliberate

- **The "Goes with" tiles use the thumbnail.** The plan says leave "the item-detail hero" on the cutout — right, but the hero is one of that screen's five images; the other four are 68px tiles and were most of its bytes.
- **`encodeThumb` returns `null`** instead of falling back to its source like `encodeCutout` does. Storing a full-size image as `thumb.webp` would double bytes for zero gain; null makes the failure path and the legacy path the same path.

## Also fixed, pre-existing

`measure shell vs complete` was waiting on a `Profile` heading that PR #45 deliberately removed. It had been timing out for 30s on every `npm run e2e:measure`.

## Found, not fixed

**4 orphaned storage objects** — 30 `cutout.webp` files for 26 items. Deleting an item leaves its blobs behind. Small now, unbounded over time, and it's the same egress question this plan serves. Not in scope; say the word and I'll do it separately.

The confirm screen has **no cancel button** — the only exits are browser-back, the nav, or closing the app. So there's no abandon event to hook, and adding a Cancel button would be inventing UI nobody designed (the exact mistake `docs/STATE.md` records from the Profile shell).

The proportionate fix is a sweep that covers *every* abandonment path — including the crashes a Cancel button would miss.

A **480px WebP derivative, generated in the browser at upload**, from the cutout, stored as `thumb.webp` beside it. Zero per-view cost, one-time client CPU — the same bargain as Decision 2's on-device background removal.

## Measured, production build, same probe before and after

| surface | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| closet grid | 493.5 kB | **97.8 kB** | −80% |
| diary month | 211.5 kB | **41.9 kB** | −80% |
| item detail | 352.5 kB | **126.4 kB** | −64% |
| stylist flat-lay | 211.5 kB | 211.5 kB | unchanged, deliberately |

The flat-lay and the item-detail **hero** keep the full cutout — they are the product. Item detail's remaining 126.4 kB is exactly the hero at full quality plus four thumbnails.

Image bytes are egress, and egress is the one unmeasured input in the break-even model (`MONETISATION.md` §7).

## Why not `next/image`

The codebase already rejected it, with a better argument than the one I arrived with (`components/closet/item-card.tsx:25`): the optimizer caches by URL, our signed URLs rotate by design, so every view would be a billed transformation on an image already compressed at upload. Supabase Storage transformations lose to the same objection, and move work off the device Decision 2 deliberately put it on.

## Decisions

- **`maxPx` 480, one derivative** — measured, not picked. The tallest masonry cell renders a ~125×160 CSS px box, which is 375×480 at DPR 3. The other consumers are far under (goes-with tile 204, diary cell 162), so one asset serves all three; a second would double upload work and storage for a few kB.
- **`original.jpg` kept.** It is 74% of stored bytes and *almost zero egress* — `displayPath` only reaches it when background removal failed. Storage is not the binding constraint; deleting it is irreversible and leaves a failed cutout unrecoverable.
- **`encodeThumb` returns `null`** rather than falling back to its source the way `encodeCutout` does. Storing a full-size image as `thumb.webp` doubles bytes for zero gain. Null leaves `thumb_url` null, so the failure path and the legacy path are one path.
- **`displayPath(item, "thumb" | "full" = "full")`** grows a size rather than gaining a sibling. `"full"` stays the default so every existing caller is unchanged; a surface opts *in* to the smaller image.

## Deviation from the plan, recorded not hidden

Task 3 says leave "the item-detail hero" on the cutout — right, but the hero is **one** of that screen's five images. The other four are `w-[92px]` "Goes with" tiles (a 68 CSS px box) and were most of its bytes. A 68px tile is exactly the "pixels are wasted" case that task is named for, so they render the thumbnail and the hero does not.

## Three traps this hit, so nobody hits them twice

1. **The storage folder is NOT `items.id`.** `uploadAndTag` mints its own `crypto.randomUUID()` for the path while the row gets a different id from its column default. The first backfill built paths from `item.id` and put all 26 thumbnails in folders holding nothing else — which still *works*, because `thumb_url` points at them, and is silently wrong. Paths derive from `cutout_url` now.
2. **`.map(displayPath)` was point-free at all five call sites**, so the new optional `size` argument would have received the **array index**. It would have survived by luck (`0 !== "thumb"`) and broken the day the parameter order changed. `tsc` caught it; all five are explicit lambdas.
3. **The diary measured ZERO images at first** — its only seeded wear is fixed at `2026-01-15` and `/calendar` renders the current month. The plan's own "measure the right thing" trap.

## Abandoned uploads, found and fixed here

`scripts/sweep-orphan-uploads.ts` — dry-run by default. Reclaimed 8 objects / 1.5 MB locally.

These are **not** deleted items: there is no delete path in the product (`lib/billing/tiers.ts`), pieces are archived, and an archived row still owns its objects. They are abandoned captures — the two-phase capture uploads both blobs *before* any row exists, so backing out of the confirm screen strands them forever. Two of the four found locally were 40 seconds apart.

- A **Cancel button is the wrong fix twice**: that screen has no such control, so it means inventing UI nobody designed — and it would still miss every crash, closed tab and dead connection.
- **Considered and rejected:** moving the upload to confirm-time would remove the orphan class outright (`tagItem` takes base64, not a storage path), but the client would re-send ~800 kB of base64 at confirm, which already crowds the Server Action body limit.
- ⚠️ **The age guard is load-bearing.** A capture in flight looks exactly like an orphan. Nothing modified within `--min-age-hours` (default 24) is considered — **verified with a negative test** at `--min-age-hours=99999`, where all four candidates were correctly left alone.
- It **reports** unreferenced files inside live folders without touching them, and that report immediately caught litter from this branch's own measurement fixture.

## Verification

- 757 unit tests · 27 e2e · `tsc` clean · `build` clean · `npm run insights` clean
- lint **identical to main's baseline** (13 problems both sides, none in touched files)
- **Visually checked on a booted iPhone 17 Pro simulator against the real 26-piece closet** — grid, diary and "Goes with" all sharp, and the diary's colour recall holds at 45px, which is its whole purpose
- The `@measure` probe had to be taught to measure at all: the e2e seed uploads 70-byte 1×1 PNGs, so a byte comparison against it reports a triumphant ~0% change. It borrows a real cutout/thumb/original triple and restores, and throws loudly rather than silently measuring one pixel
- Local storage after: 33 items, 33 cutouts, 33 originals, 27 thumbnails, **zero orphans, zero strays**
- Also fixed, pre-existing: `measure shell vs complete` waited on a `Profile` heading PR #45 deliberately removed, and had been timing out for 30s on every `npm run e2e:measure`

## Migration

`20260824090000_item_thumb.sql` adds `items.thumb_url`, **nullable** — load-bearing, since every existing row predates it. Run `npx tsx scripts/backfill-thumbs.ts --apply` after deploy (idempotent, dry-run by default; 26 items locally, 2454.7 kB of cutouts → 319.4 kB).

Grounded now. The headline: **we pass `removeBackground(original)` with no config at all**, so we're on the library's defaults — `model: "medium"` (`isnet_fp16`, half precision) on `device: "cpu"`.

And your shoe shows the specific failure that follows from it: the dark panel behind the swoosh is the *same value as the backdrop*, so the model reads it as background and eats a hole clean through the interior. That's black-on-black separation failing, not edge quality.

Ranked by value per unit of effort:

**1. Contrast guidance at capture — free, biggest lever.** No matting model separates a black panel from a black backdrop. The viewfinder already says "on a flat surface"; saying *"on a surface that contrasts with the piece"* costs one string. A capture-time check (sample the border colour, compare to the subject's dominant colour, warn before spending the WASM run) is a small step beyond that.

**2. `model: "large"` → `isnet` full-precision.** One config line. Better interior coherence and edges than fp16; costs a larger one-time model download, which we already cache. This is the cheapest code-only quality bump and the first thing I'd measure.

**3. Stop feeding the model a compressed JPEG.** `processImage` compresses to 0.5 MB/1280px *first*, then segments that. Compression artefacts hurt matting for the same reason `encode.ts` holds the cutout at 0.85 for the tagger — and here we've already degraded the input before the model ever sees it. Segmenting the original `file` and compressing after is a small reorder.

**4. Fill interior holes in the alpha mask.** `output.format: "image/x-alpha8"` returns the raw mask, and a flood-fill from the image borders identifies any transparent region *not* connected to the edge — by definition interior. Fixes your shoe exactly. ⚠️ But it has a real trade-off I won't paper over: a genuine see-through gap — inside a tote handle, a belt buckle, between straps — is *also* interior and not border-connected, so blanket filling would wrongly solidify those. It needs a size threshold tuned against your actual closet, which means measuring, not assuming.

**5. `device: "gpu"` (WebGPU).** Mainly makes option 2 affordable rather than improving quality itself. Needs a capability check and a CPU fallback; iOS Safari support is the open question.

**6. A touch-up brush on the confirm screen.** The honest endgame — Decision 3 already says "AI is ~90% right; the user fixes the rest," and that screen exists for precisely this. But it's real UI that nobody has designed, so it wants a design pass first, not a patch.

My recommendation: **2 and 3 together as one measurable experiment**, re-run against a handful of your real problem items (that shoe included), before touching mask post-processing. They're two config-level changes with no new UI and no new failure modes, and if they fix the shoe then 4's trade-off never has to be taken.

Worth saying plainly: I haven't measured any of this yet — the whole point of the pairing is that 2 and 3 are cheap enough to *test* rather than argue about. Want me to set that up as a scoping doc, or just run the experiment on a few of your items?

# Cutout quality — scoping

> **Not a TDD plan.** Research and open decisions. A plan written from this before the decisions in
> §6 are made would be rewritten. Raised by a user report: a blue Jordan 1 Low came back with a hole
> eaten through its interior, the dark backdrop showing through around the swoosh and collar.

---

## 1. ⚠️ The finding that outranks the quality question

**`@imgly/background-removal` is AGPL-3.0, and it is on the critical path of every capture.**

Its own README, verbatim:

> *"The software is free for use under the AGPL License. Please contact support@img.ly for questions
> about other licensing options."*

That is textbook dual licensing: AGPL as the free tier, a commercial licence for everyone else. The
library is downloaded and executed **in the user's browser**, which is conveying it, and AGPL's
copyleft reaches the work it is combined with. Fitcheck is a closed-source product with a planned
€5 paid tier (`MONETISATION.md`).

**This is the same class of problem as Open-Meteo** — a free-tier dependency that is not licensed for
the commercial product being built, sitting on a path every user walks. `docs/STATE.md` already calls
Open-Meteo *"the only item that can stop a launch."* There are now two.

### The escape route is unusually clean

`ThirdPartyLicenses.json` in the installed package lists everything IMG.LY builds on:

| dependency | type | licence |
|---|---|---|
| `onnxruntime-web` | code | **MIT** |
| **ISNET** (`github.com/xuebinqin/DIS`) | **model** | **MIT** |
| `ndarray`, `zod`, `lodash-es` | code | MIT |

**Every ingredient is MIT. Only IMG.LY's wrapper is AGPL.** So the same model, at the same quality,
can run on `onnxruntime-web` directly with no AGPL anywhere — the dependency is replaceable without
changing the segmentation at all.

⚠️ **I am not a lawyer, and this is a legal call, not an engineering one.** What is established here
is factual: the licence text, the dual-licence offer, and that the substrate is MIT. Whether AGPL
actually reaches Fitcheck's bundle is the decision — and it has exactly three answers: buy IMG.LY's
commercial licence, replace the wrapper, or accept the risk deliberately and in writing.

---

## 2. What is actually wrong with the cutouts today

### 2a. We pass no configuration at all

`lib/images/process.ts` calls `removeBackground(original)` with no second argument. The library's
schema (`dist/src/schema.d.ts`) shows what we are therefore defaulting into:

| option | default we get | also available |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | `"medium"` → **`isnet_fp16`** (half precision) | `"large"` → `isnet` (fp32), `"small"` → `isnet_quint8` |
| `device` | **`"cpu"`** | `"gpu"` (WebGPU) |
| `output.format` | `image/png` | `image/x-alpha8` — **the raw mask** |
| `rescale`, `proxyToWorker` | defaults | — |

Three levers we have never touched, on the feature the whole product depends on.

### 2b. The reported failure is black-on-black, not weak edges

The shoe has a dark panel behind the swoosh, photographed against a dark backdrop. ISNet cannot
separate them, so it labels interior pixels as background and punches a hole through the silhouette.

⚠️ **This matters for choosing a fix.** A bigger model narrows this case; it does not eliminate it.
No matting model reliably separates a black object from a black background — that is an information
problem in the photograph, not a capacity problem in the network. **The cheapest real fix is at
capture time, not inference time.**

### 2c. We segment an image we have already degraded

```ts
const original = await imageCompression(file, compressionOptions());  // 1280px, 0.5MB, JPEG
const raw = await removeBackground(original);                          // ← the COMPRESSED blob
```

We hand the model a re-compressed JPEG. `lib/images/encode.ts` already documents why this is bad,
for the tagger: *"heavy compression introduces artefacts that hurt model accuracy."* The same is true
of matting, and here we do it before the model ever sees the picture. Segmenting `file` and
compressing afterwards costs memory and time, and costs nothing in money.

### 2d. We throw the mask away

The library hands back a composited PNG. With `output.format: "image/x-alpha8"` we would get the
alpha mask itself, which is what every post-processing technique needs. Today we cannot inspect,
threshold, feather or repair anything, because by the time we see the result the decision is baked in.

---

## 3. ⚠️ The user's half of the problem, which is larger than the model's

Reading the capture flow end to end, the model is not the weakest link.

### 3a. Nothing tells the user what makes a good photo

`components/capture/viewfinder.tsx` shows framing corners and *"Tap to capture an item"*. The only
guidance is one line below it: *"Snap each piece on a flat surface."* **Nothing mentions contrast** —
the single variable that decides whether §2b happens. A user photographing black jeans on a dark sofa
is set up to fail and never told.

### 3b. The confirm screen shows the damage and offers no way to act on it

`ConfirmForm` renders the cutout large, on `.surface-stage`. If the cutout has a hole, **this is where
the user sees it** — and the screen has exactly one action: **Save**. There is no retake, no reject,
no touch-up. The only escape is to navigate away.

Two consequences:

1. **The user's only options are to accept a damaged image or lose the capture.** Most will accept it,
   and the closet quietly fills with broken cutouts that surface later on the flat-lay and the grid.
2. **Backing out strands the upload.** Both blobs are already in Storage before any row exists — the
   orphan class fixed on `feat/image-weight` (PR #46). Two of the four found locally were 40 seconds
   apart, which reads exactly like *capture → see a bad cutout → back out → retry → back out.*
   **The abandoned-capture bug and the cutout-quality bug are the same user, twice.**

⚠️ And a subtlety worth keeping: `.surface-stage` is a **dark** radial gradient, so a hole that has
punched through to transparency renders **dark on dark at review time** and is easy to miss — then
becomes obvious later on a different surface. The review screen is the one place that should make a
hole loud, and its styling does the opposite.

### 3c. "No cutout" is already a supported state, and nobody uses it

`lib/storage/signed.ts`:

```ts
export function displayPath(item: ImageRow, size = "full") {
  if (size === "thumb" && item.thumb_url) return item.thumb_url;
  return item.cutout_url ?? item.image_url;   // ← falls back to the ORIGINAL PHOTO
}
```

A row with `cutout_url: null` renders the original photograph, everywhere, correctly. The reader
already handles it; the backfill already skips such rows; RLS and paths are unchanged. So **"keep the
photo instead of a broken cutout" needs no schema change and no migration** — only a button that
passes `cutoutPath: null` to `confirmItem`. That is the single cheapest quality win available, and it
is a product decision, not an engineering one.

---

## 4. The options, honestly costed

| # | Option | Quality | Cost / risk | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | **Contrast guidance at capture** (copy, then optionally a border-vs-subject check) | Prevents the worst case entirely | One string; the check is small | — |
| B | **Reject / retake / "keep the photo"** on the confirm screen | Stops bad cutouts entering the closet | Needs design; also closes the orphan path | — |
| C | **`model: "large"` (isnet fp32)** | Modest, real | One line; bigger one-time model download | AGPL unless §1 resolved |
| D | **Segment the original, not the compressed JPEG** | Modest, real | Reorder two lines; more memory/time | AGPL unless §1 resolved |
| E | **`device: "gpu"` (WebGPU)** | None directly — buys the headroom for C | Capability check + CPU fallback | AGPL unless §1 resolved |
| F | **Take the mask (`x-alpha8`) and repair it** — flood-fill interior holes | Fixes §2b directly | ⚠️ See the trap below | AGPL unless §1 resolved |
| G | **Own the pipeline on `onnxruntime-web`**, ISNet weights | Same as today, plus everything F needs | ~150 lines we maintain | **MIT — clears §1** |
| H | **BiRefNet (MIT), lite ONNX ~214 MB, 1024×1024** | Best available client-side | ⚠️ See the onboarding trap | **MIT** |
| I | **Server-side or third-party API** (remove.bg, Photoroom, Supabase transforms) | High | Per-image cost forever | — |

### ⚠️ The trap in F, stated before anyone implements it

"Fill any transparent region not connected to the image border" fixes the shoe. It also **fills
legitimate holes**: the gap inside a tote handle, a belt buckle, the space between a strap and a
shoulder, the negative space in an open cardigan. Those are interior and not border-connected too.
It needs a size threshold tuned against the **real closet**, and it must be measured, not assumed.

### ⚠️ The trap in H, and it is a product trap not a technical one

`done/2026-07-16-onboarding-five-capture.md` — **the first five items are captured during onboarding,
before the user has ever seen the magic moment.** A 214 MB model download at that moment is an
activation catastrophe. CLAUDE.md's Decision 2 already accepts "a few-MB first-load model download";
214 MB is two orders of magnitude past that.

**If BiRefNet is ever wanted, it cannot be the onboarding model.** The shape that works is
tiered: ship the small model for the first captures, and offer the heavy one later — as an opt-in
"re-cut this item in high quality" on item detail, downloaded on demand, for the pieces that matter.
That also happens to be a natural **Pro** surface.

---

## 5. What the future makes more expensive

Cutout quality gets *more* load-bearing, not less:

- **Share cards (`@vercel/og`, Phase 2).** The cutout leaves the app and becomes marketing. A hole in
  a shoe is a private annoyance today and a public one then.
- **Women's wardrobe** (`scoping/2026-07-24-womens-wardrobe-scoping.md`). One-piece garments, thin
  straps and sheer fabric are the hardest matting cases that exist. The current model will be worse
  there than it is on menswear, and that fork is where the complaints will arrive.
- **pgvector / CLIP (Phase 4).** Visual similarity is computed from the image. Holes corrupt
  embeddings silently — the failure mode is bad recommendations nobody can trace to a cutout.
- **The 50-piece free closet cap.** Every wasted capture spends one of fifty. A broken cutout the user
  cannot reject costs them 2% of their free allowance.

---

## 6. Recommendation

**Two tracks, because §1 is a decision and §2–3 are work.**

### Track 1 — decide the licence (blocking, not engineering)

Answer §1 before spending anything on C/D/E/F, all of which deepen the investment in an AGPL
dependency. Three options: buy IMG.LY's commercial licence, do **G** (own the pipeline on
`onnxruntime-web`, all-MIT), or accept the risk deliberately and record it.

**My recommendation: G.** It costs ~150 lines, removes a launch blocker, and is a prerequisite for
F anyway — the mask access, the input resolution and the execution provider all come with it. It
turns a legal problem and a quality problem into one piece of work.

### Track 2 — ship the user-side fixes now, they are licence-independent

**A and B, in that order**, and neither touches the model:

1. **A** — say "on a contrasting surface" in the viewfinder. One string, prevents the reported failure.
2. **B** — give the confirm screen a way out: *Retake* and *Keep the photo instead* (the latter is
   free, per §3c). This stops bad cutouts entering the closet, and closes the abandoned-upload path
   that PR #46 currently has to sweep up afterwards.

Then, once Track 1 lands: **D** (segment the original) → **C/E** (bigger model, GPU where available)
→ measure → only then consider **F**, with the threshold tuned on the real closet.

**H stays out of scope** until someone wants a Pro "re-cut in high quality" surface, and it must never
be the onboarding model.

---

## 7. Open decisions — for the user, not the implementer

1. ⚠️ **The AGPL question. Buy, replace, or accept?** This is the one that blocks a paid launch, and
   it is the same shape as the Open-Meteo decision still sitting open.
2. **Does the confirm screen get a Retake / "Keep the photo" control?** It is new UI on a designed
   screen — `docs/STATE.md`'s Profile lesson says do not invent UI, so this wants a design pass, not
   a patch. But the screen is currently a dead end, which is its own design bug.
3. **Is a "re-cut this item" action wanted at all** — free, or the Pro surface H would suit?
4. **How much first-load download is acceptable during onboarding?** Decision 2 says "a few MB". That
   number decides which models are ever on the table.

## 8. What was checked, so it is not re-derived

- `@imgly/background-removal@1.7.0`, `LICENSE.md` = AGPL-3.0; README offers commercial licensing.
- `ThirdPartyLicenses.json`: `onnxruntime-web` MIT, **ISNET model MIT** (`xuebinqin/DIS`), rest MIT.
- `ConfigSchema`: `model` defaults to `"medium"` → `isnet_fp16`; `device` defaults to `"cpu"`;
  `output.format` accepts `image/x-alpha8`.
- `lib/images/process.ts` passes **no config**, and segments the **compressed** blob.
- `displayPath` already falls back to `image_url` when `cutout_url` is null.
- `ConfirmForm` has exactly one action (Save) — no retake, no reject, no touch-up.
- BiRefNet is MIT; `BiRefNet_lite` ONNX ≈ 214 MB at 1024×1024.
- ⚠️ **Not measured:** the actual quality delta of C, D or E on the real closet. Nothing in §4 above
  claims a measured improvement, and it should not be quoted as if it did.

content.text:
I need to correct something I told you an hour ago, because it changes the decision.

**I said the escape route was "unusually clean — everything under it is MIT, including the ISNet weights."** I took that from IMG.LY's `ThirdPartyLicenses.json`. Verifying it against the source, that manifest is not reliable:

| source | licence claimed for the *same* ISNet weights |
|---|---|
| IMG.LY's `ThirdPartyLicenses.json` | MIT |
| the actual DIS repo (`xuebinqin/DIS`) | **Apache-2.0** — "our code and evaluation metric use Apache License 2.0" |
| `onnx-community/ISNet-ONNX` on HuggingFace | **AGPL-3.0** |

And the more important part IMG.LY's manifest doesn't mention at all: the pretrained weights were **trained on DIS5K**, which ships a separate `DIS5K-Dataset-Terms-of-Use.pdf`. Academic segmentation datasets routinely restrict commercial use, and the repo licence covers the *code*, not the data the weights were learned from.

Three sources, three licences, plus an unread dataset term. That's worse than a clearly restrictive licence, because you can't plan around ambiguity.

## So: is there a free model?

Free *libraries*, yes — `onnxruntime-web` (MIT), Transformers.js (Apache-2.0). Those are genuinely unencumbered. **The scarce thing is weights with clean provenance.**

| model | licence | commercial | fit for flat-lay garments |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ISNet** (what we run) | contested — see above | unclear | good, it's what we use |
| **RMBG-1.4 / 2.0** (Bria) | explicitly non-commercial | ❌ needs a Bria licence | good — but ruled out |
| **BiRefNet** | MIT repo, authors permit commercial | likely ✓, same DIS5K question on weights | best quality; 214 MB lite |
| **ormbg** | Apache-2.0, **deliberately trained on openly-licensed data** to dodge exactly this | ✓ cleanest provenance found | ⚠️ **optimised for humans**, wrong domain |
| **U²-Net** | Apache-2.0 | ✓ code; DUTS-TR data is research-only | older, weaker |

`ormbg` is the only one built specifically to have clean provenance — and it's the one whose *domain is wrong*, since it's tuned for people, not garments on a surface.

## The honest conclusion

There is no option here whose weight provenance is unambiguously clean for a commercial product. **That's precisely why IMG.LY, Bria, Photoroom and remove.bg all sell licences** — the market exists because the free path is legally murky, not because the models are hard to run.

Which leaves three real choices, and this one is genuinely a lawyer's call, not mine:

1. **Buy IMG.LY's commercial licence.** Certain, and it *preserves Decision 4* — it's a flat SDK licence, not per-image, so the on-device zero-marginal-cost economics survive intact. Cost unknown; worth an email to find out.
2. **Run BiRefNet or ISNet yourself on `onnxruntime-web`** and accept the residual dataset-terms risk knowingly. Removes the AGPL wrapper question entirely, still doesn't fully resolve the weights question.
3. **Get actual advice on the DIS5K terms and whether AGPL reaches your bundle.** Both are cheap questions for a lawyer and expensive ones for us to keep guessing at.

Recorded as a decision in the scoping doc (§12) and `STATE.md`.

## One thing to be straight about first

**Free cannot buy certainty here.** Every remaining option is legally amber — even the non-DIS5K models train on academic corpora (DUTS, ECSSD, HKU-IS) whose commercial rights are *undocumented* rather than *granted*. Bria and Prama sell indemnity precisely because nobody else can offer it. So the goal shifts to **minimising residual risk, not eliminating it** — better said now than discovered later.

What free *can* remove is the two things that are concretely written down: the **AGPL exposure** (clearly enforceable per FSF guidance and *Artifex*) and the **explicit non-commercial DIS5K clause** (an actual prohibition, not an ambiguity).

## Track A — free, and keeps today's quality

1. **One email to the DIS authors** for the DIS5K commercial terms-of-use their project page says is *"free of charge for the current version."* If granted, the written non-commercial clause stops applying to you — and it covers you regardless of how the "do dataset terms bind downstream users" question resolves.
2. **Replace the AGPL wrapper** with our own `onnxruntime-web` (MIT) pipeline. ~150 lines. Removes the AGPL half entirely, keeps ISNet so **no quality regression**, and unlocks segmenting the original + keeping the mask in the same change.

Cost: one email and one focused piece of engineering.

## Track B — only if DIS doesn't answer or says no

| | licence | trained on | ONNX | size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **InSPyReNet** | MIT | standard SOD, **no DIS5K** | ❌ we'd export it | unpublished |
| **u2netp** | Apache-2.0 | classic saliency, **no DIS5K** | ✅ ready | **4.7 MB** |

**InSPyReNet is the more interesting one** and it's missing from every "just use rembg" answer, because it needs an ONNX export nobody has published. That export *is* the cost of Track B. u2netp is the safe-but-weaker option — though 4.7 MB is a much better onboarding budget than what you ship today.

## Ruled out

**BiRefNet and BEN2** — free of charge, but **DIS5K-trained**, so they carry the exact clause Track A exists to remove, at 20× the download. Free of charge is not free of the clause. **ormbg** is free and clean-ish but human-optimised, so wrong domain for flat-lays.

## Unchanged either way

The contrast line in the viewfinder and a way out of the confirm screen. Free, licence-independent, and they fix the complaint that actually started this — your shoe. **Ship them regardless of how Track A goes.**

Without it there's nothing to ask permission for, and any permission he granted would be worthless because he'd have been answering a different question.

Now #3 — let me be concrete about what I'm actually proposing, because it's two different things solving two different problems.

**Retake** = discard this capture, back to the viewfinder. For *"let me try a better photo."* It would also delete the uploaded blobs on the way out — which closes the abandoned-upload leak **at source**, instead of sweeping it up afterwards.

The guidance said *"on a flat surface"* and never mentioned **contrast** — the single variable that decides whether background removal succeeds.

The confirm screen renders the cutout large, which makes it **the one place a bad cut is visible** — and it offered exactly one action, *Add to closet*. The choice was to save a damaged image or navigate away.

Three lines in, three lines out. What it does:

1. **Reset first** — `setDraft(null)`, `setPhase("aim")`. You're back at the viewfinder immediately, before any network call.
2. **Then clean up** — delete the staged blobs.
3. **If that delete fails, say nothing.**

## What the `catch` actually costs

Two things, and only one of them is covered:

- **The blobs stay orphaned.** Covered — `scripts/sweep-orphan-uploads.ts` reclaims them, which is exactly what it exists for.
- **Nobody ever learns it failed.** Not covered. There's no log, no counter. If this failed for 30% of users you'd find out from the sweep reporting more files than expected, and not before.

The second is the real weakness. I accepted it because there's currently nowhere to send that signal — PostHog is Phase 2 per `CLAUDE.md`, so the alternative today is a `console.error` nobody reads.

## Why swallow rather than retry or surface

- **Surfacing it** would put an error on a screen you've already rejected, about a cleanup you didn't ask for and can't act on. That's the "stranding you" case — strictly worse than the leak.
- **Retrying** is speculative machinery for a failure I haven't observed once, and the sweep already handles the outcome.

## When I'd revisit it

When analytics land (Phase 2) — then the `catch` becomes a one-line event instead of a comment, and you'd know the real failure rate rather than assuming it's negligible. That's a genuinely better version, it just needs a destination to exist first.

Verified as-is: the happy path deletes everything (proven end-to-end in WebKit with a real photo, zero files left behind), and a test pins that a *failing* cleanup still returns you to the viewfinder with no error shown.

# Own the cutout pipeline — drop the AGPL wrapper

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan
> task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Run the same segmentation we run today, on our own `onnxruntime-web` (MIT) pipeline, and
delete `@imgly/background-removal` (AGPL-3.0) from the bundle. **No quality regression** — that is the
acceptance criterion, not a hope.

**Architecture:** Replace one library call with four steps we own — decode → preprocess → ONNX session
→ postprocess. Same ISNet model, same input size, same output shape. Everything stays client-side; the
zero-marginal-cost bargain of Decision 2 is unchanged.

**Tech Stack:** TypeScript 6, `onnxruntime-web` (MIT), WebAssembly / optional WebGPU, Canvas, Vitest,
Playwright/WebKit.

---

## Why this exists, and what it does NOT fix

`@imgly/background-removal` is **AGPL-3.0** and dual-licensed (*"contact support@img.ly for questions
about other licensing options"*). It is downloaded and executed in every user's browser, which the
**FSF's own guidance** treats as *conveying* — legally like shipping a binary, not like SaaS. The FSF
licence FAQ further holds that JavaScript combined into a single program with AGPL code puts the whole
combined work under copyleft absent an explicit exception, and IMG.LY grants none. *Artifex v. Hancom*
established that these licences are enforceable as contract **and** copyright, and Artifex runs the
identical dual-licence business model.

Full analysis: `scoping/2026-08-25-cutout-quality-scoping.md` §1, §9b.

⚠️ **This plan does NOT resolve the DIS5K question.** The weights were trained on a dataset whose
Terms of Use are non-commercial by default. That is a **separate problem with a separate owner**, and
it is addressed by the permission request in `docs/dis5k-permission-request.md`, sent 2026-08-25.
**Do not conflate them.** This plan removes the AGPL half — the half we control, and the half the case
law actually touches.

⚠️ **If the DIS answer comes back "no"**, the model swaps but this pipeline does not: Task 2 exists
precisely so the model is a parameter rather than a premise. See §Task 6.

---

## ⚠️ Read this first — the failure mode that matters

**The whole risk of this plan is a silent quality regression.** The user's original complaint was a
cutout with a hole in it; shipping a rewrite that quietly makes *every* cutout slightly worse would be
a far bigger defect than the one we set out to fix, and **no test in this repo would catch it.**

Preprocessing is where it will go wrong, and the errors are all invisible in a type system:

- **Normalisation.** ISNet expects specific mean/std handling. Get it wrong and you get plausible,
  uniformly worse masks — not a crash.
- **Channel order** (RGB vs BGR) and **layout** (NCHW vs NHWC).
- **Resize interpolation** on the way in, and on the way back out to the source resolution.
- **Output selection.** ISNet emits multiple side outputs; the first is the one to use. Taking the
  wrong one produces a coarse mask that still looks like a mask.

**Task 1 exists so these are measured against the current library rather than reasoned about.**

---

### Task 0: Pin the current behaviour before changing anything

**Files:** `lib/images/__tests__/fixtures/`, `e2e/` measurement only

- [ ] **Step 1:** Choose **8–10 real garments from the developer's closet** spanning the hard cases:
  a black item on a dark ground (the reported failure), a white item on a pale ground, something with
  a thin strap or handle, something with a genuine interior hole, a patterned piece, and a shoe.
  ⚠️ **Not stock photos.** The whole point is the distribution this product actually sees.

- [ ] **Step 2:** Run each through the CURRENT `@imgly` path and save the resulting cutouts as
  reference artefacts, with their byte sizes and alpha coverage (proportion of non-transparent pixels).
  ⚠️ **These are the baseline the rewrite is judged against.** Without them "no regression" is a
  feeling.

- [ ] **Step 3:** Record the current model download size and the wall-clock time of `processImage` on
  a real device, so Task 5 can prove we did not make onboarding slower.

### Task 1: A characterisation harness

**Files:** `lib/images/__tests__/segmentation-parity.test.ts`, `scripts/compare-cutouts.ts`

**Interfaces:** `alphaCoverage(blob: Blob): Promise<number>`, `maskIoU(a: Blob, b: Blob): Promise<number>`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the comparison first.** Intersection-over-Union between two alpha masks, plus

  disjoint → 0.0, half-overlap → 0.5) **before** any real image is involved.

```ts
export type SegmentModel = { url: string; inputSize: number; mean: number[]; std: number[] };
export async function segment(source: Blob, model: SegmentModel): Promise<Blob>;  // RGBA cutout
export async function segmentMask(source: Blob, model: SegmentModel): Promise<ImageData>;  // raw alpha
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Decode + preprocess.** `createImageBitmap` → canvas at `model.inputSize` → `Float32Array`

  literal**, so Task 6's model swap is a config change rather than a rewrite.

- [ ] **Step 3: Run the session.** `ort.InferenceSession.create` with the WASM execution provider.
  ⚠️ **Cache the session across captures** — the onboarding flow captures five items in a row, and
  re-creating the session each time would pay the setup cost five times.

- [ ] **Step 4: Postprocess.** Take the FIRST output, min-max normalise it, resize the mask back to
  the SOURCE resolution (not the model resolution), and write it into the alpha channel of the
  original pixels. ⚠️ **Never fill the canvas** — same rule as `lib/images/thumb.ts`, and for the same
  reason: a white matte behind every garment looks perfect in a byte count and ruins every screen.

- [ ] **Step 5:** Expose `segmentMask` as well as `segment`. It costs nothing here and it is the seam
  every future quality fix needs — hole-filling, feathering, thresholding — none of which are possible
  today because the library hands back a composited PNG (`scoping/…` §2d).

**Files:** `public/models/`, or a documented CDN decision

- [ ] **Step 1:** ⚠️ **Do not fetch weights from IMG.LY's CDN.** That is their asset served under
  their terms, and continuing to pull from it while claiming to have removed the dependency would be
  the worst of both worlds.

- [ ] **Step 2:** Obtain the ISNet ONNX weights from a source whose licence we have actually read, and
  **record which one, in this file, with the licence text at the time of download.**

  (`scoping/…` §9d) — this is the step where that gets pinned down instead of hand-waved.

- [ ] **Step 3:** Decide where it is served from and write the reason down. Bundling in `public/`
  means Vercel bandwidth on every first run; a CDN means a third party. ⚠️ **Whatever is chosen, the

- [ ] **Step 4:** ⚠️ **Measure the download against onboarding.** The first five items are captured
  *during* onboarding, before the user has seen the magic moment. If this is materially larger than
  what `@imgly` fetches today, say so out loud rather than shipping it quietly.

**Files:** `lib/images/process.ts`, `package.json`

- [ ] **Step 1:** Replace `removeBackground(original)` with `segment(...)` in `processImage`.

- [ ] **Step 2:** ⚠️ **Segment the ORIGINAL file, not the compressed JPEG.** Today `processImage`

  compression hurts model accuracy, and here we do it before the model ever sees the image

  separately from the parity check: run Task 1 both ways, and report both numbers.

- [ ] **Step 3:** **Remove `@imgly/background-removal` from `package.json`** and confirm it is gone

  dependency installed has achieved nothing legally.

- [ ] **Step 4:** Grep the repo for any remaining reference, including comments and docs, and update

- [ ] **Step 1:** `npm run test:run && npx tsc --noEmit && npm run build && npm run lint && npm run e2e`
  and `npm run insights`.

- [ ] **Step 2:** ⚠️ **The parity table, every row, in the PR.** IoU per fixture against the Task 0
  baseline. **If any fixture regresses, do not ship it** — say which one and why.

- [ ] **Step 3:** ⚠️ **Look at the cutouts, in the iOS Simulator, on the dark stage.** IoU is a number;
  a halo, a jagged edge or a white matte is a thing you have to see. The diary and closet grid render
  these at 45–160px and the item-detail hero renders one full size — check both ends.

- [ ] **Step 4:** Re-run the Task 0 timing on a real device. Onboarding captures five items in a row;
  a pipeline that is correct and twice as slow is a different kind of regression.

- [ ] **Step 5:** ⚠️ **Drive a real photo end-to-end in WebKit**, as PR #47 did — file input through to
  the confirm screen — so the tested path is the shipped path rather than a unit-tested approximation.

---

**Files:** `lib/images/segment.ts` config only

- [ ] **Step 1:** If the DIS permission request is refused or unanswered, swap `SegmentModel` to a
  non-DIS5K model — **InSPyReNet** (MIT) or **u2netp** (Apache-2.0, 4.7 MB). Task 2 Step 2 is what

- [ ] **Step 2:** ⚠️ **Re-run Task 1's parity table against the CURRENT baseline, and expect it to be
  worse.** `scoping/…` §9g: the legally safest free model is a *lower-quality* model, and trading
  cutout quality for legal comfort in a product built on cutouts is a real cost that must be seen
  before it is accepted.

- [ ] **Step 3:** Put the numbers in front of the user and let them choose. **This is a product
  decision, not an implementation detail.**

---

## Open decisions — for the user, not the implementer

1. **Where do the weights get served from** — bundled in `public/` (our bandwidth) or a CDN (a third
   party)? Task 3 Step 3.
2. **How much first-run download is acceptable?** Decision 2 says "a few MB". If our own hosting of
   ISNet lands materially above what `@imgly` fetches today, that number needs revisiting — and it

   the table published; identical output is not achievable across different runtimes anyway.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/1curafu/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.3.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
the approval gate never does.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
artifact, never the approval.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
