# Packing Mode — Scoping

_Scoped 2026-07-24. **Not a plan.** Brainstorm the open decisions before writing one._

## Question

The design sells Pro on three features (`Fitcheck.dc.html:697`): *"Unlimited daily looks, **packing
mode** & cost-per-wear analytics."* Two of those exist as plans. What is packing mode?

## Answer

Nobody has said. It appears **once**, inside a marketing sentence on a card — no screen, no data model,
no mention in `fitcheck-complete-spec.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/prototype-review.md`, or any plan. It is
the only Pro feature with no specification at all.

That makes it the highest-uncertainty item in the queue and the reason this is a scoping doc rather than
a plan.

## Why it is worth building anyway

Of the six Pro features in `docs/MONETISATION.md`, packing mode is the only one with a **deadline
attached** — you need it *this week, before the flight*. Deadline-driven features convert far better
than open-ended benefits, and the urgency is recurring without being constant.

It is also episodic, so it does not inflate steady-state serving cost, and its output — a laid-out
capsule wardrobe for a trip — is the most screenshot-shareable thing the product could produce.

## The likely shape

A trip goes in, a capsule and a schedule come out:

**Input:** destination, dates, and the occasions expected (work / everyday / evening / weekend, probably
weighted — "3 work days, 2 evenings").

**Output, two parts:**
1. **The capsule** — the *minimum set of items* that can dress every day of the trip. This is the real
   product. "Take these 9 pieces" is worth more than any individual outfit.
2. **A look per day**, drawn from that capsule, matched to the destination's forecast.

## What already exists that this reuses

Genuinely a lot — this is more assembly than invention:

| Need | Already built |
|---|---|
| Destination weather | `lib/weather/` — Open-Meteo + geocoding, forecast by coordinates |
| Occasion → formality band | `lib/generator/rules.ts` (`personalBand`, `applyFormalityOverride`) |
| Building and scoring outfits | `lib/generator/` — candidates, colour, score, rank |
| Naming a look + the why | `lib/generator/rerank.ts` |
| Persisting a set of outfits | `lib/outfits/` — the daily-drop write path generalises |
| Gating it | `lib/billing/entitlements.ts` (`packingMode`) once the entitlements plan ships |

## The one genuinely new algorithm

Everything above produces outfits **one at a time and independently**. A capsule is the opposite: a
*set* problem, where the goal is maximum outfit coverage from minimum items, and the pieces must be
chosen together because they have to recombine across days.

That is set cover — NP-hard in general, trivially fine at wardrobe scale with a greedy heuristic
(repeatedly add the item that unlocks the most still-uncovered days). Worth knowing it is a different
kind of problem from anything in `lib/generator/` today, because a plan that assumes "just run the
generator N times" will produce N unrelated outfits needing 3N items — which is the opposite of packing.

Note the shape is close to the **gap analysis** in the wear-stats plan (also "which item unlocks the
most?"). Whichever ships first should expose its primitive for the other.

## Open design decisions (brainstorm these before writing a plan)

1. **Is laundry modelled?** A 10-day trip with 4 shirts implies re-wearing. Does the capsule assume
   re-wear, and does it say so? This single answer changes the capsule size dramatically.
2. **Is the capsule editable?** If the user removes a piece, does the schedule re-solve around it? An
   un-editable capsule will be wrong for anyone with a real trip.
3. **How does it handle "I don't own it"?** The generator can only pack what is in the closet. If the
   trip needs formality the wardrobe cannot reach, does it say so plainly, or fall back to the closest
   thing? (This project has fixed the "silently returns nothing" failure three times already — see
   `personalBand`, outerwear, seasons.)
4. **Persistence.** Is a trip an entity — `trips` + `trip_items`, revisitable and editable — or a
   one-shot render? Anything worth £5/mo should be revisitable while you are actually packing.
5. **Cost.** One trip = one multi-day generation. Is it one Pro generation, several, or unmetered
   because it is Pro-only anyway? Affects `entitlements`.
6. **How much AI?** The capsule solve should be deterministic (cheap, explainable). The model's job is
   naming and the *why*, as everywhere else. Confirm — the temptation to hand the whole trip to the
   model is real and would be expensive and unreliable.
7. **Does it need destination context beyond weather?** "Amalfi in August" and "Frankfurt in August"
   share a forecast and not a dress code. Probably out of scope for v1; worth saying so explicitly.

## Rough scope (once designed)

Assuming decisions 1-7 land near the simple end:

- Migration: `trips` + `trip_items` (or reuse `outfits` with a trip key)
- `lib/packing/capsule.ts` — the greedy set-cover solve, pure and unit-tested
- `lib/packing/schedule.ts` — assign a look per day from the capsule
- Server action + `/packing` route + trip-input form
- Two screens: the trip setup, and the capsule + day-by-day result
- Entitlement gate + the limited state

Mid-sized — bigger than `fit-diary`, smaller than the generator itself. Most of the risk is in decisions
1 and 3, not in the code.

content.text:
Good question, and it's the right instinct — but let me be precise, because "merge" hides the actual decision.

**Merging isn't bad. It's the only version that works.** Neither half stands alone:

- **Capsule alone** = *"take these 9 pieces."* You still have to work out combinations each morning — which is the exact problem Fitcheck exists to remove. You'd have shipped a packing list, not a stylist.
- **Days alone** = 7 good outfits that between them need 21 items. That isn't packing; that's the daily drop with a different date range and a suitcase you can't close.

So they're not two features to merge — they're **one pipeline with two outputs**. The capsule is the *constraint*, the daily looks are the *payoff*. Option 3 in my list was that merge; I framed it poorly.

**The real decision is which one the algorithm optimises for**, because they pull against each other:

| | optimises | fails as |
|---|---|---|
| **Capsule-first** | smallest suitcase | some day gets a mediocre outfit, because pieces were chosen for coverage, not for looking good together |
| **Days-first** | best outfit each day | the capsule bloats — you packed for 7 great days and it's 18 items |

There's a third shape that dissolves the tension, and I think it's the right one: **solve them together.** Greedy set-cover, but a piece only counts as "covering" a day if it takes part in an outfit that scores above a quality floor. You get the minimum capsule *subject to* every day still being good. It's barely harder than plain greedy — one extra condition in the loop — and it means neither output is sacrificed to the other.

That also happens to reuse the scoring already in `lib/generator/score.ts`, so the quality floor isn't a new concept we'd have to invent.

**My recommendation: merged, solved together, with the capsule shown first** — because "9 pieces" is the line that sells the feature and the thing worth screenshotting, while the days are what you actually open each morning of the trip.

One thing I'd flag: this is still the *biggest* of the three builds. If you'd rather ship something in a week than something complete, days-first (a trip-shaped daily drop) reuses almost everything and needs no new algorithm at all — and you could add the capsule solve later without rework, since the days would already exist to dedupe.

So: **merged and solved together** (fuller, differentiated, ~the scoping doc's scope), or **days-first now, capsule later** (fast, safe, less special)?
so actually it would be better to merge and solve together, so we woulnd lose a thing, or im wrong?

You're right that it loses nothing **in the product** — nothing gets sacrificed, and the capsule and the days each make the other worth having. Let me just be straight about what it *does* cost, so it's a choice rather than a hope:

- **Time.** It's the biggest of the three builds. Real, but see below.
- **A tuning parameter.** The quality floor has to be set against your actual closet. Too high and no capsule is ever small; too low and some day is mediocre. This project's history is unkind here — the wear-stats gap card was rebuilt **three times** against real data because an invented threshold looked fine until it met a real wardrobe.
- **More surface for the failure case.** If the closet genuinely can't dress the trip, a merged solve has more ways to fail quietly. That's scoping decision #3, and this codebase has fixed "silently returns nothing" three times already (`personalBand`, outerwear, seasons).

None of those are reasons not to do it. They're the things to design *for*.

And one fact makes the timing easy: **there's no deadline.** Packing mode is advertised in the upgrade sheet, but nothing can be bought — Stripe is #17, after everything. So the "ship fast" argument has nothing to buy you. **That's the strongest case for doing it properly the first time**, which is your instinct.

So: **merged, solved together, capsule shown first.** Agreed.

---

Next decision, and the scoping doc calls it the one that changes capsule size most:

**Does the capsule assume you re-wear things?**

A 10-day trip with 4 shirts obviously means re-wearing. The question is whether the app *models* that and *says so*.

- **Assume re-wear, silently** — smallest capsule, but the user opens it, counts 4 shirts against 10 days, and doesn't trust it.
- **Assume re-wear, and say so** — the day view shows "Oxford shirt, 2nd wear". Honest, and it's the thing that makes a small number believable. Costs a little UI.
- **Never re-wear** — one fresh set per day. Trustworthy, and produces a capsule so large it defeats the point.
- **Let the user set it** — "laundry available" toggle, or "re-wear after N days".

My recommendation is **assume re-wear and show it**, because the number 9 is only persuasive if the user can see *how* 9 covers 7 days. A capsule that doesn't explain itself gets ignored in favour of the suitcase they'd have packed anyway.

Which way?
so add re-wear and maybe also let user set it, like maybe he want to wear it 3 times, idk

Good instinct, and thinking it through, the user control isn't optional — a single global number produces an absurd capsule.

If "wear each item twice" applied flatly to a 7-day trip, you'd get ~4 tops (fine), ~4 bottoms (questionable) and **~4 pairs of shoes** (nobody packs that). Shoes and outerwear re-wear almost indefinitely; tops re-wear least. So:

**Per-category defaults, with one control that shifts the whole scale.**

| category | default max wears |
|---|---|
| Outerwear | whole trip |
| Shoes | whole trip |
| Bottoms | 3–4 |
| Tops | 2 |

The user control then moves that curve rather than setting a flat number — one dial, from *pack light* to *pack fresh*. Sliding toward light stretches every category; toward fresh, tightens them.

And there's an existing pattern that fits this exactly. `DESIGN.md`'s **labelled meter**: uppercase kicker left, plain-language value right, five segments with the filled ones in rust — *"never a number on its own, always the word."* It's what the formality control already uses:

```
RE-WEAR                        Up to twice
■  ■  □  □  □
```

So the control is on-system rather than invented, which matters given how much of this feature has no design of its own.

Two things that follow, worth naming now:

- **The day view shows the wear count** — *"Oxford shirt · 2nd wear"*. That's what makes a 9-piece capsule believable instead of suspicious.
- **Laundry falls out for free.** "Pack light" *is* "I'll do laundry." No separate toggle needed, which keeps the trip setup to one screen.

## 2. Colors: The Midnight Atelier Palette

A warm near-black canvas, a cream text ramp, and one terracotta voice.

### Primary
- **Terracotta Rust** (#B86A47): The single accent. Reserved for meaning — the active nav tab, checkmarks and progress fill, the AI badge, the brand-colored `J` glyph before stylist reasoning, links, and focus rings. It is a highlight, not a fill.
- **Rust High** (#D69873): The lighter rust for text on tinted rust surfaces (selected chips) and hover lifts of rust elements.
- **Rust Deep** (#9A5236): Pressed/active rust states; doubles as the destructive tone — even errors stay in the palette's warmth.

### Neutral
- **Canvas** (#0E0E10): The body background everywhere. Warm near-black, never `#000`.
- **Surface 1–3** (#161517 → #19181B → #201F22): The elevation ramp. Cards sit on Surface 1, popovers on Surface 2, hover surfaces on Surface 3. Depth is tonal, not shadowed.
- **Cream** (#EDE6D8): Default foreground text and the fill of primary buttons. **Cream-Strong** (#F3EEE3) for display headings that need extra presence.
- **Warm Gray** (#928C7F): Secondary text — captions, inactive nav labels, the reasoning line's muted variant. Passes 4.5:1 on Canvas; this is the dimmest color allowed for readable text.
- **Warm Gray Dim / Faint** (#615C52 / #52504A): Decorative only — kickers, disabled labels, hairline ornaments. Never body copy.

### Tertiary
- **Style-DNA swatches** — Navy (#2C3A4C), Camel (#B89A6A), Olive (#6E6F52), plus Cream and Rust: the tonal wardrobe-palette swatches shown on the Style DNA screen and in data viz (`--chart-*`). Not general-purpose UI colors.

### Named Rules
**The One Rust Rule.** Terracotta Rust appears on at most ~10% of any screen. Primary buttons are cream-filled with dark text — never rust-filled. If a screen has more than one rust-dominant element competing, remove one.

**The No-Pure-Black Rule.** `#000000` and `#FFFFFF` are forbidden. The darkest value is Canvas #0E0E10; the lightest is Cream-Strong #F3EEE3.

**The Readability Floor.** Warm Gray #928C7F is the minimum for text a user must read. Dim and Faint are ornament.

## 3. Typography

**Display Font:** Libre Caslon Text (serif fallback) — 400, 700, and 400 italic, loaded via `next/font/google` as `--font-serif`
**Body Font:** Hanken Grotesk (system-ui fallback) — 300–700, loaded as `--font-sans`

**Character:** A classic high-contrast serif against a warm, quiet grotesk — the pairing of a fashion magazine masthead and its picture captions. The serif carries identity and voice; the sans disappears into function.

### Hierarchy
- **Display** (Caslon 400, ~4.5rem, 0.92 line-height, −0.02em): The wordmark and welcome-screen moments only.
- **Headline** (Caslon 400, 1.875rem, 1.12 line-height, −0.01em): Screen titles — "The Closet", "Today's Looks".
- **Reasoning** (Caslon 400 *italic*, ~1.0625rem): The stylist's "why it works" line and taglines, led by a Terracotta Rust `J` glyph. This is the product's voice — it is never truncated, never shrunk to caption size.
- **Body** (Hanken 400, 1rem, 1.5): All functional copy. Cap prose at 65–75ch.
- **Label / Kicker** (Hanken 500, 11px, +0.22em, UPPERCASE, Warm Gray Dim): Micro-labels like "19 PIECES". The brand kicker variant on the welcome screen runs 13px, +0.34em, in rust.

### Named Rules
**The Italic Why Rule.** AI stylist reasoning is always serif italic with the rust `J` glyph — hero treatment, not a caption. Any new surface that shows an outfit inherits this treatment unchanged.

**The Two-Voices Rule.** Serif speaks (identity, titles, reasoning); sans works (buttons, forms, data). Never set UI controls in the serif; never set a screen title in the sans.

=== DON'Ts ===
### Don't:
- **Don't** make anything look "playful, cute, or a generic SaaS dashboard" — PRODUCT.md's words. If a screen reads as a settings panel, it has failed.
- **Don't** use gamified badge-and-streak visual language, even where streak mechanics exist.
- **Don't** use gradient text, glassmorphism-as-decoration, or hero-metric layouts — the "generic AI-product look" PRODUCT.md forbids.
- **Don't** use drop shadows, pure black, pure white, or rust-filled primary buttons.
- **Don't** set body copy in Warm Gray Dim (#615C52) or Faint (#52504A) — they fail contrast; #928C7F is the floor.
- **Don't** truncate, shrink, or de-italicize the stylist reasoning line — it is the product, not a caption.
- **Don't** add a light theme, colored category badges, or new accent hues; the Style-DNA swatches are data, not UI colors.

# Packing Mode — design brief

_Written 2026-08-26, for generating screen concepts. Companion to
`superpowers/plans/scoping/2026-07-24-packing-mode-scoping.md`._

## There is no existing design. That is the point of this document.

Packing mode appears **once** in `design_handoff_stylist_generator/Fitcheck.dc.html`, inside a
marketing sentence on the upgrade card (`:697`): *"Unlimited daily looks, packing mode &
cost-per-wear analytics."* No screen, no data model, no mention in the spec. It is the only Pro
feature with no specification at all.

⚠️ **So these screens must be derived, not invented.** The user's decision of 2026-07-28 — *"we should
still follow this detail page for cloth, it's the best"* — makes **item detail**
(`Fitcheck.dc.html:587-657`) the parent for any screen without a design of its own. A concept in a
different visual register is worse than no concept: it produces something attractive that we then
cannot build, and the drift catalogued in `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` started exactly that way.

---

## The screens

### 1. Trip setup

The only input screen. One screen, not a wizard.

| shows | notes |
|---|---|
| Destination | ⚠️ **Reuses the existing location picker** — one component already serves Settings and the Stylist's weather pill (queue #9c). Do not draw a new one. |
| Date range | Start and end. The day count is the number everything else is sized against. |
| Occasion mix | The product's **four fixed occasions** — work, everyday, evening, weekend. Weighted, e.g. "3 work, 2 evening". Do not invent a fifth. |
| **RE-WEAR meter** | The labelled-meter pattern: uppercase kicker left, **plain-language value right**, five segments with filled ones in rust. `RE-WEAR … Up to twice`. ⚠️ Never a bare number — that is a named rule. |
| One primary | Cream pill, full width: *"Plan the trip"*. |

### 2. The capsule — the hero screen

This is the product. *"Take these 9 pieces"* is the line that sells the feature and the thing worth
screenshotting.

| shows | notes |
|---|---|
| Kicker | `LISBON · 12–18 MAY` — wayfinding, uppercase, letterspaced, muted. |
| Serif headline | **The number.** "Nine pieces." Caslon, large, cream. The number is the headline; it is not a stat tile. |
| Stat tile row | Three rounded surfaces, serif value over uppercase micro-label: `9 / PIECES`, `7 / DAYS`, `14 / OUTFITS`. The established pattern from item detail. |
| **The capsule itself** | Cutouts, and they are **the largest elements on screen**. Generous negative space. The clothes speak; the UI whispers. |
| **The why line** | ⚠️ Serif *italic*, led by the rust `J` glyph — *why these nine work together*. **The Italic Why Rule is mandatory**: any surface showing an outfit inherits it unchanged, never truncated, never shrunk to caption size. |
| One primary | *"See the days"*. |

### 3. Day by day

| shows | notes |
|---|---|
| Per day | Date, occasion, destination weather, the look as a flat-lay. |
| **Wear counts** | `Oxford shirt · 2nd wear`. ⚠️ **This is what makes a 9-piece capsule believable** rather than suspicious. Without it the user counts 4 shirts against 7 days and stops trusting the output. |
| The why line | Per look, same italic treatment. |

### 4. The closet cannot dress this trip

⚠️ **Required, not an edge case.** This project has fixed "silently returns nothing" **three times**
(`personalBand`, outerwear, seasons). If the wardrobe cannot reach the formality or warmth a trip
needs, the screen says so plainly and names what is missing. It never quietly returns a short capsule
and lets the user discover the gap at the airport.

---

## Non-negotiable system rules

From `DESIGN.md`. A concept that breaks these cannot be built.

**Palette — "The Midnight Atelier"**
- Canvas `#0E0E10` (warm near-black). Surfaces ramp `#161517 → #19181B → #201F22`.
- Cream `#EDE6D8` text and **primary button fills**; Cream-Strong `#F3EEE3` for display headings.
- Warm Gray `#928C7F` secondary text — **the dimmest colour allowed for anything readable**.
- Terracotta Rust `#B86A47` — **the single accent**.

**The named rules**
- ⚠️ **One Rust Rule** — rust on **at most ~10%** of any screen. **Primary buttons are cream-filled with dark text, never rust-filled.** Two competing rust elements means removing one.
- ⚠️ **No-Pure-Black Rule** — `#000000` and `#FFFFFF` are forbidden.
- ⚠️ **Italic Why Rule** — stylist reasoning is serif italic with the rust `J` glyph. Hero treatment, not a caption.
- ⚠️ **Two-Voices Rule** — serif speaks (titles, identity, reasoning), sans works (buttons, forms, data). **Never a screen title in the sans; never a UI control in the serif.**
- ⚠️ **Hairline Rule** — cards bounded by cream at 7–12% opacity. **No drop shadows anywhere.** Depth is the tonal ramp.

**Type**
- Display/titles: **Libre Caslon Text**. Body/controls: **Hanken Grotesk**.
- Kicker: Hanken 500, 11px, +0.22em, uppercase, Warm Gray Dim.

**Format**
- **Mobile only. 390×844.** Fitcheck is a phone PWA — there is no desktop layout, and a desktop-width
  comp has already produced a false finding on this project once.

## Don'ts

- ❌ Playful, cute, or generic-SaaS-dashboard. *"If a screen reads as a settings panel, it has failed."*
- ❌ Gamified badge-and-streak language — even though streaks exist elsewhere.
- ❌ Gradient text, glassmorphism-as-decoration, hero-metric layouts — the "generic AI-product look".
- ❌ Drop shadows, pure black/white, rust-filled primary buttons.
- ❌ Colored category badges or any new accent hue.
- ❌ A light theme.

## The vocabulary to inherit, in order

From the canonical item-detail screen: **brand kicker → serif display title → grotesk subtitle with
`·` separators → stat tiles → labelled meter → hairline spec table → horizontal cutout card row →
bottom action bar (one small secondary icon + one full-width cream pill)**.

Two things that screen encodes and are easy to lose: **cutouts are the hero and everything else is
quiet around them**, and **the rust accent appears exactly once**.

---

## How to generate

Use the **`imagegen-frontend-mobile`** skill — images inside phone mockups, no code, cheap to throw
away. Generate screens 1–3 first; screen 4 only once the others are settled.

⚠️ Generate **one image per screen**, not a composite sheet. Each needs to be judged at phone size.

The brief is above. The short version:

## Four screens

2. **The capsule** — the hero. *"Nine pieces"* as a serif headline, stat tiles (9 pieces / 7 days / 14 outfits), the cutouts as the largest things on screen, and the italic why line.

And the anti-brief, straight from `PRODUCT.md`: *if a screen reads as a settings panel, it has failed.* No gamified badges, no gradient text, no hero-metric dashboard look.

## On generating it

Everything without a design of its own derives from **item detail** — your own call on 2026-07-28, *"we should still follow this detail page for cloth, it's the best."* A concept in a different register is worse than none: it produces something attractive we then can't build, and that's exactly how the drift in `design-review-2026-07-24.md` started.

Re-check your working files afterwards (background task if you can) and say so in everyday words. ## Updating an existing canvas Seeding is not one-shot — updates re-run it: - **A canvas you authored this session**: keep your working files (`Main.dc.html`, siblings, images, `canvas.json`). To change anything, edit the working files and re-run step 2 — the helper always seeds a FRESH copy of `payload.template.html`; never edit or re-seed the already-seeded output file (the never-read-the-payload rule applies to it too). Then republish the same path (step 4's republish rule). Adding an image is the same move: downsample it, pass it with `--image`, reference it by filename, re-seed. - **A canvas that lives on the Artifact** (the user edited it in the GUI and saved, or it is from another session): WebFetch the artifact URL. Ignore the inline head the result shows (that is editor code — do not read further into it); the result names a file where it saved the full page. If the extracted set has no `Main.dc.html` (the user deleted that artboard in the GUI), re-seed it as it is — the helper warns and the editor uses the first artboard by name as the entry; never rename an artboard to manufacture a Main. The first response is always the same: WebFetch the artifact again, `--extract` the freshly saved page into a new directory, redo your edit on those files, re-seed, and republish normally — that picks up their save instead of discarding it. Only if THAT republish is still refused for want of a document version you can target (a canvas other writers have saved reads back unversioned, so every ordinary republish of it is refused) — and your re-seed was built from that complete, fresh `--extract`, never from the inline head — tell the user in one line that the canvas carries other people's saves and ask whether anyone is still editing; on their go-ahead, republish once with `force: true`. If someone is mid-edit, wait and repeat the fresh read first: forcing over an edit you have not read back discards it. ## Artboards and canvas.json Every `.dc.html` file in the document is an artboard on the canvas. Click an artboard's title to select it; drag the title to move it; "+ Artboard" in the edit toolbar adds one. Click into an artboard to focus it — the properties panel and tools bind to the focused artboard. Copy/paste moves elements between artboards (select → ⌘C → click the other artboard → ⌘V; template `{{ holes }}` stay holes and re-resolve against the destination's logic). `canvas.json` is the layout manifest, a files entry: ```json { "artboards": [ { "file": "Hero.dc.html", "x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 880, "h": 560 }, { "file": "Main.dc.html", "x": 960, "y": 0, "w": 560, "h": 640 } ], "annotations": [ { "id": "brief-summary", "x": 40, "y": -120, "w": 240, "text": "Sticky-note text" } ], "launch": { "view": "canvas" } } ``` - `x`/`y`/`w`/`h` are CSS px on the infinite canvas (at zoom 1). `w`/`h` set the artboard FRAME size — they neither scale nor crop the content, so match them to your root element's fixed size (a 720×1080 root in a 560-wide frame scrolls/clips inside the frame; it does not shrink). `$preview` in data-props is a separate, component-level preferred-size hint — setting both to the root's size is correct, not redundant. Four more per-artboard fields exist: `title` (a cosmetic display rename for the artboard header; the file stem stays the identity everywhere), `expand` (`"fit"` default | `"fill"` — the expanded view's Fit toggle starts on: the whole artboard on black, shrunk to fit if larger; `"fill"` starts it off: the frame is resized to the window and the page scrolls, so give that artboard a fluid-width root), `print` (`"fixed"` default | `"flow"` — the artboard's print mode, also editable in the editor under Artboard settings), and `page` (which page the artboard belongs to — see `pages` below; omit on a single-page canvas). - **Print design** is a first-class use of this format: author each page as an artboard. For fixed-pagination pieces (brochures, posters, single-page docs), use a SERIES of single-page artboards, one per page, each with `"print": "fixed"` (or omitted — fixed is the default). For document-like pieces (memos, reports), use a SINGLE flowing artboard with `"print": "flow"` — its content may paginate across as many printed pages as it needs. The flow-vs-fixed distinction is consumed ONLY by print/PDF pagination, which the Design editor does not implement yet (today's Export PDF rasterizes every artboard as exactly one page) — seed it anyway so documents carry the right intent when that path lands. - Omitted `.dc.html` files get slots appended automatically; an omitted canvas.json lays every artboard out in a row. Artboard STEMS must be unique (case-insensitively; the helper refuses duplicates). **There is no way to hide a `.dc.html` entry from the canvas** — component files a design imports are artboards too, and omitting one from canvas.json just appends it back. Treat that as the component-library view: give component artboards a deliberate spot (e.g. a row below the mains) rather than fighting it. - `launch` picks the view a fresh open lands on. Exactly two shapes are accepted: `{"view": "canvas"}` (the artboard canvas — with an optional `"page": ""` to open on that page; absent means the entry artboard's page) and `{"view": "focused", "file": ""}` (that artboard alone in the window — see `expand`; its own page is the one shown, so it carries no `page`). The helper refuses a launch the editor would ignore — an unknown view, a focused file not in the artboard list, a page that is not listed. The editor also writes it implicitly: expanding an artboard records the focused shape and collapsing records the canvas shape (dirty until Save like any edit); and every Save stamps the page that is open, so a document reopens on the page it was last saved from. When canvas.json has `pages`, set `launch` to `{"view": "canvas", "page": ""}` on every seed and re-seed, so the user opens on the current work. - `annotations` are sticky notes: top-level canvas objects alongside the artboards, with NO backing file — manifest-only data. Each entry is exactly `{id, x, y, w, text}` plus an optional `page` as for artboards (no other keys — the helper refuses them): `id` a UNIQUE handle of 1–40 letters, digits, `-`/`_` (the editor drops a note whose id is anything else or repeats an earlier one — read the existing ids before adding; notes made in the GUI are `note-1`, `note-2`, …; at most 200), `x`/`y`/`w` in canvas px (width 120–960; height always auto-fits the text, so there is no `h`), `text` ONE plain string (newlines as `\n` inside it — never an array of lines; ~5000-char cap; control characters are stripped). In the editor: the Note tool in the edit sidebar's insert cluster (key N) places one; drag moves it, the right-edge grip sets width, double-click edits text in place, Delete removes it — each its own undo step. Notes do not join artboard copy/paste (⌘C/⌘V) or the PNG/PDF exports yet. Omit the key when there are none (an empty list is dropped on save). - `pages` (optional) splits the canvas into named pages the viewer flips between from the toolbar's pages menu (each row carries a Rename button for viewers who can save). List order is menu order — it never picks the page a fresh open shows; `launch`'s `page` does (above). Omit `pages` entirely for a single-page canvas (the default; do not add it just to name one page). # Prompt for Claude Design — Packing Mode

_Copy everything inside the fence. Self-contained: Claude Design has no access to the repo._

---

````markdown
Design four mobile screens for **Fitcheck**, an AI wardrobe stylist PWA. Phone only — **390×844**,
one artboard per screen. No desktop layout, no fake iOS status bar.

Fitcheck digitises someone's wardrobe and suggests outfits from clothes they already own. This
feature is **Packing Mode**: you tell it where you're going and for how long, and it works out the
smallest set of clothes that can dress every day of the trip, then assigns a look to each day.

The visual system below is real and already shipped across the rest of the app. **Follow it exactly**
— these are lifted values, not suggestions. New screens must look native beside the existing ones.

## The design system — "The Midnight Atelier"

Warm near-black canvas, a cream text ramp, one terracotta voice.

**Colour**
- Canvas `#0E0E10` — the body background everywhere. Warm near-black.
- Surfaces `#161517` → `#19181B` → `#201F22` (cards → popovers → hover)
- Cream `#EDE6D8` — default text, and the fill of primary buttons
- Cream strong `#F3EEE3` — display headings only
- Value `#CFC8BA` — the right-hand side of every label/value pair
- Warm gray `#928C7F` — secondary text. **The dimmest colour allowed for anything readable.**
- Warm gray dim `#615C52` — kickers and ornament only, never body copy
- Rust `#B86A47` — the single accent. Rust-high `#D69873`, rust-deep `#9A5236`

**Type** — both are Google Fonts
- **Libre Caslon Text** (serif): screen titles, identity, stylist reasoning
- **Hanken Grotesk** (sans): all controls, forms, data, labels
- Screen title: Caslon 400, 30px, line-height 1.12, −0.01em
- Reasoning: Caslon 400 **italic**, ~17px
- Body: Hanken 400, 16px, 1.5
- Kicker: Hanken 500, **11px, letter-spacing 0.22em, UPPERCASE**, `#615C52`

**Elevation — flat and tonal, no shadows anywhere**
Every raised surface carries an inset cream hairline: `inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(237,230,216,α)`
where α steps 0.03 / 0.05 / 0.06 / 0.07 / 0.08 / 0.10 / 0.12 by elevation. Depth comes from the
surface ramp, never from a drop shadow.

## Components — exact specs from the shipped app

**Primary button** — `border-radius 12px`, background `#EDE6D8`, padding 17px vertical, text
`#0E0E10`, weight 600, full width. **Never rust-filled.**

**Secondary icon button** — 54px tall × 56px wide, `border-radius 14px`, background `#19181B`,
`inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(237,230,216,0.10)`, 19px stroke icon in `#928C7F`.

**Bottom action bar** — sticky, 12px gap, 22px side padding, 14px top padding, over a gradient from
canvas (60%) to transparent. **One small secondary icon + one full-width primary. One primary action
per screen.**

**Stat tile** (rows of three) — `border-radius 13px`, background `#161517`, padding 14px,
`inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(237,230,216,0.05)`. Value in **Caslon 15px** on top, label beneath in
**10px uppercase, letter-spacing 0.1em, `#615C52`**, bottom-aligned.

**Chip** — `border-radius 999px`, padding 17px horizontal / 12px vertical, 14px medium.
*Filter chips*: active = cream fill with canvas text; inactive = 12% cream border, transparent.
*Select chips*: active = rust border at 50%, rust background at 15%, text `#D69873`.

**Labelled meter** — uppercase kicker on the left, **plain-language value on the right**, then five
segments with the filled ones in rust. Example: `FORMALITY … Smart casual`.
**Never a bare number — always the word.**

**Spec table** — rounded 14px container on `#161517`, hairline-divided rows, muted label left, value
right in `#CFC8BA`, multi-values joined with `·`.

**Cutout stage** — aspect ratio 1.3, `border-radius 18px`, a radial gradient lit from above
(not a flat fill). Garment cutouts float on it with generous padding.

**Garment card** — the cutout floats on the card's gradient with ~20px padding; brand name above in
11px uppercase `#615C52`; item name below in **Caslon 15px `#CFC8BA`**.

## The named rules — a design that breaks these can't be built

1. **One Rust Rule** — rust on **at most ~10% of any screen**. Primary buttons are cream-filled with
   dark text, **never rust-filled**. If two rust-dominant elements compete, remove one.
2. **No Pure Black or White** — `#000000` and `#FFFFFF` are forbidden. Darkest is `#0E0E10`,
   lightest `#F3EEE3`.
3. **Italic Why Rule** — the stylist's "why this works" line is **always Caslon italic, led by a rust
   `J` glyph**. It is hero treatment, never a caption, never truncated, never shrunk.
4. **Two Voices** — serif speaks (titles, identity, reasoning), sans works (buttons, forms, data).
   Never a screen title in the sans; never a UI control in the serif.
5. **Hairline Rule** — cards bounded by cream at 7–12% opacity. **No drop shadows.** If a surface
   needs separation, step up the tonal ramp.
6. **Readability floor** — `#928C7F` is the dimmest colour for text anyone must read.

**Cutouts are the hero; everything else is quiet around them.** The clothes should be the largest
elements on screen, with real negative space. The UI whispers.

## The four screens

### 1. Trip setup
The only input screen. One screen, not a wizard.
- Destination (city) and a date range
- **Occasion mix** — the app's four fixed occasions: **work, everyday, evening, weekend** — weighted,
  e.g. "3 work days, 2 evenings". Don't invent a fifth occasion.
- **A RE-WEAR labelled meter**: `RE-WEAR … Up to twice`, five segments, filled in rust. This is how
  the user trades suitcase size against freshness.
- One cream primary: "Plan the trip"

### 2. The capsule — the hero screen
This is the product. "Take these nine pieces" is what sells the feature.
- Kicker: `LISBON · 12–18 MAY`
- **Serif headline: the number.** "Nine pieces." Large Caslon, cream. It is the headline, not a tile.
- Stat tile row: `9 / PIECES`, `7 / DAYS`, `14 / OUTFITS`
- **The capsule itself** — the garment cutouts, the largest thing on screen, generous negative space
- **The why line** — Caslon italic with the rust `J`: why these nine work together
- One cream primary: "See the days"

### 3. Day by day
- One entry per day: the date, the occasion, the destination's weather, and the look as a flat-lay
  of cutouts
- **Wear counts on each piece** — `Oxford shirt · 2nd wear`. This is what makes nine pieces
  believable rather than suspicious, so it must be visible, not buried.
- The italic why line per look

### 4. "Your closet can't dress this trip"
A required state, not an edge case. When the wardrobe can't reach the formality or warmth the trip
needs, this screen **says so plainly and names what's missing** — e.g. "You have nothing formal
enough for two evenings out." It never silently returns a short capsule. Keep it calm and useful,
not an error page: offer the nearest thing it *can* build.

## Don'ts

- Nothing playful, cute, or generic-SaaS. **If a screen reads as a settings panel, it has failed.**
- No gamified badges, streak flames, or progress-bar celebration.
- No gradient text, glassmorphism-as-decoration, or big hero-metric dashboard layouts — the
  "generic AI product" look.
- No drop shadows, no pure black or white, no rust-filled primary buttons.
- No coloured category badges and no new accent hue. Rust is the only accent.
- No light theme.
- No emoji, and no emoji-as-icons — draw stroke icons on a 20/24px grid instead.
- Touch targets never below 44px.

Start with the capsule screen — it's the one that has to be beautiful. Then trip setup, then day by
day, then the empty state.
````

---

## Notes for you

- **Screen 2 is the one to judge first.** If the capsule doesn't feel special, the feature isn't
  worth building — everything else is supporting cast.
- The prompt deliberately does **not** describe the layout of the capsule itself. That's the actual
  open design question, and prescribing it would just get my guess back in nicer pixels.
- Where a real value is missing (which nine garments, real trip dates), Claude Design will invent
  plausible ones. That's fine for a concept — just don't let invented outfit content become a
  requirement later.

Read it — and it's good. Let me check it against the actual token values I lifted earlier rather than trusting my own prompt back.

**The fidelity is genuinely exact.** These aren't approximations:

| element | the design | the shipped app |
|---|---|---|
| Stat tile | `13px` radius, `#161517`, `14px` pad, inset `.05` | `rounded-[13px] bg-surface-1 p-[14px] hairline-2` ✓ |
| Stat value | Caslon `15px`, `line-height:1` | `font-serif text-[15px] leading-none` ✓ |
| Secondary icon btn | 56×54, `14px`, `#19181B`, inset `.10`, 19px icon | `h-[54px] w-14 rounded-[14px] bg-surface-2 hairline-6`, `size={19}` ✓ |
| Primary pill | `12px`, `#EDE6D8`, `17px` pad, 600 | `rounded-[12px] bg-foreground py-[17px] font-semibold` ✓ |
| Bottom bar | `14px/22px/26px`, gap 12, gradient at 60% | `pt-[14px] px-[22px] gap-3 from-canvas from-60%` ✓ |
| Kicker | 11px, `.22em`, `#615C52` | `kicker.tsx` exactly ✓ |

It could be pasted into the codebase with almost no translation.

## What's genuinely strong

**The shortfall screen is the best thing here.** It doesn't just refuse — it names what's missing *and why it matters* ("One dark blazer — it alone turns four of your shirts into evening looks"), then offers **"What it can build: a five-day capsule"** with `7 pieces / 5 days / 2 uncovered`. That's the "never silently return nothing" requirement solved better than I'd specified it.

**The re-wear meter carries a hint per position** — *"The sweet spot: seven days out of nine pieces, nothing worn tired."* It teaches the trade-off instead of just setting a number.

**It's interactive** — the occasion mix has working +/− with a 7-day cap, the meter is clickable, and wear-counts are a toggle. Touch targets are 44px.

## ⚠️ It quietly answered four open scoping decisions

Worth surfacing before they harden by default:

- **#4 Persistence** — "Save packing list" means trips are **saved entities**. That implies `trips` + `trip_items` tables.
- **#2 Editable capsule** — there's **no edit affordance anywhere**. The capsule is take-it-or-leave-it.
- **#7 Destination context** — weather only, no dress code. Confirms v1 scope.
- **#5 Metering** — nothing indicates cost, so it reads as unmetered-because-Pro.

Those are reasonable answers. They just shouldn't become decisions by accident.

## Small drift worth fixing

- **The garment colours near-miss your own tokens.** It uses `#C6A374` camel and `#33455B` navy; you have `--color-dna-camel: #B89A6A` and `--color-dna-navy: #2C3A4C`. The Style-DNA swatches exist for exactly this.
- **A few invented greys** — `#3A3A3D`, `#2E2D31`, `#241D18` aren't in the ramp.
- **Trip setup has no back control** while the other three do.
- **Day-by-day is the rust-heaviest screen** — three occasion labels in `#D69873` plus two `J` glyphs. Worth eyeballing against the ~10% rule.
- The page backdrop is `#08080A`, darker than Canvas — but that's presentation chrome around the artboards, not app UI, so it doesn't ship.

## Where that leaves us

Three of the seven scoping decisions are now genuinely settled (#1 re-wear, #3 shortfall, #7 context), and four were answered implicitly. ## #7 — What it is

**Lisbon in May and Frankfurt in May can share a forecast and share nothing else.** One is a beach city, the other is a banking city — same 20°C, completely different dress codes.

**My answer: no, and you already solved it.** The **occasion mix is the dress code.** A user going to Frankfurt says "5 work days"; a user going to Lisbon says "2 work, 3 everyday, 2 evening". They've told us what they'll be doing, which is more reliable than us guessing from a city name — and it needs no data source we don't have. Worth writing down as a deliberate no, so nobody re-opens it later.

## #5 — Metering: do we need it?

The cost is small: the capsule solve is deterministic and free, and the AI only names things and writes the "why". A 7-day trip is one or two Haiku calls, not eight. Packing is Pro-only, and Pro already means unlimited daily looks — putting a counter on it would contradict what you're selling.

## #4 — What persistence means

Does a trip get **saved to the database and reopened**, or is it generated fresh each time you look?

It matters because you don't use a packing list once. You plan on Sunday, pack on Thursday, check it at the airport, open it in the hotel. If it isn't stored, every one of those is a fresh generation — different results each time, and you'd never trust it.

**My answer: saved.** It's also the pattern you already committed to — Decision 5 says looks are generated once and persisted, and tapping an occasion *reads* rather than regenerates. The design already assumes this — that's what "Save packing list" is.

#7 but we can fetch weather to know what clothes to take #5 okay #4 okay save #2 okay

**#7 was asking about something *extra*: cultural dress code.** Should the app know "Amalfi is a beach town" versus "Frankfurt is a banking city" — two places that can share a forecast and share nothing else? - `lib/packing/rewear.ts` — per-category wear limits and how the meter shifts them

# Packing Mode — design spec

_2026-08-26. Supersedes the open decisions in `../plans/scoping/2026-07-24-packing-mode-scoping.md`,
all seven of which are now closed. Visual reference: the Claude Design project **Styling**,
`Fitcheck Packing Mode.dc.html` (four artboards, 390×844)._

## What it is

A trip goes in — destination, dates, what you'll be doing — and two things come out:

1. **A capsule**: the smallest set of pieces that can dress every day of the trip.
2. **A look per day**, drawn from that capsule and matched to the destination's forecast.

The capsule is the product. *"Take these nine pieces"* is worth more than any individual outfit,
and it is the most screenshot-shareable thing Fitcheck can produce. The days are what you open each
morning while you are there.

**Pro-only.** It is one of the three features the upgrade sheet already advertises, and the only one
with a **deadline attached** — you need it *this week, before the flight*. Deadline-driven features
convert better than open-ended ones, and the urgency recurs without being constant.

---

## The seven decisions, closed

| # | Decision | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Laundry / re-wear** | Modelled and **visible**. Per-category defaults, one meter shifts them. |
| 2 | **Editable capsule** | **Yes** — remove, pin, swap. An edit is a constraint on the same solve. |
| 3 | **Closet can't cover the trip** | A **required screen**, not an error. Names what is missing and offers what it *can* build. |
| 4 | **Persistence** | **A real entity.** `trips` + `trip_items`, revisitable and editable. |
| 5 | **Cost** | **Recorded, not limited.** Writes to `generation_events`; no quota. |
| 6 | **How much AI** | Solve is deterministic. The model only **names** and writes the **why** — one batched call per trip. |
| 7 | **Destination context beyond weather** | **No.** Weather yes; dress-code-by-city no — the occasion mix already carries it. |

### ⚠️ Why #7 is a deliberate no

Lisbon and Frankfurt in May can share a forecast and share nothing else — one a beach city, one a
banking city. Modelling that would need a dress-code data source we do not have and would be us
guessing from a city name. **The occasion mix is the dress code**, and it comes from the user:
"5 work days" and "3 everyday, 2 evening" describe the trip better than any lookup could. Recorded
here so it is not reopened as a new idea.

### ⚠️ Why #5 records without limiting

Packing is Pro-only, and Pro already promises unlimited daily looks — metering it would contradict
what is being sold. But `generation_events` is an append-only ledger that answers *"what has this
user actually spent"*, and a trip that writes nothing to it is invisible. Trips write a `trip` kind
alongside the existing `drop`, `regenerate` and `styled`. **Recording is not limiting.**

---

## Re-wear, and why it is per-category

A single global "wear each item twice" produces an absurd capsule: a 7-day trip would want ~4 tops
(fine), ~4 bottoms (questionable) and **~4 pairs of shoes** (nobody packs that). Shoes and outerwear
re-wear almost indefinitely; tops re-wear least.

**Defaults:**

| category | default max wears |
|---|---|
| Outerwear | whole trip |
| Shoes | whole trip |
| Bottoms | 3–4 |
| Tops | 2 |

**One control shifts the whole curve**, from *pack light* to *pack fresh*, rather than setting a flat
number. It renders as the design system's **labelled meter** — uppercase kicker left, plain-language
value right, five segments with the filled ones in rust — the same component the formality control
uses. ⚠️ **Never a bare number; always the word** (a named rule in `DESIGN.md`).

⚠️ **Laundry needs no separate toggle.** "Pack light" *is* "I will do laundry", which keeps trip
setup to one screen.

⚠️ **Wear counts are shown on every day** — `Oxford shirt · 2nd wear`. This is what makes a
nine-piece capsule believable rather than suspicious: without it the user counts four shirts against
seven days and stops trusting the output.

---

## The one genuinely new algorithm

Everything in `lib/generator/` today produces outfits **one at a time and independently**. A capsule
is the opposite: a *set* problem, where pieces must be chosen together because they have to recombine
across days.

⚠️ **A plan that assumes "run the generator N times" produces N unrelated outfits needing ~3N items —
the opposite of packing.**

### Greedy set-cover, with a quality floor

Repeatedly add the item that unlocks the most still-uncovered days; stop when every day is covered.
NP-hard in general, trivially fine at wardrobe scale.

**With one addition:** a day counts as covered only if its outfit clears a **quality floor**, scored
by the existing `lib/generator/score.ts`. Without it the solve optimises for a small suitcase and
buys it with a bad Wednesday. With it, the capsule is the smallest set **subject to every day still
being good** — so neither output is sacrificed to the other.

⚠️ The shape is close to the **gap analysis** in wear-stats (also "which item unlocks the most?").
Whichever is touched next should expose its primitive for the other rather than growing a second copy.

### Editing is the same solve, constrained

| edit | how |
|---|---|
| **Remove** a piece | re-solve with it excluded |
| **Pin** a piece | seed the solve with it already selected, at zero cost |
| **Swap** | a pin plus a remove |

⚠️ **Pinning is the more valuable half** — *"I bought this for the trip, build around it"* — and the
pattern is already proven here: `app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts` pins one item and generates
around it. This is the same idea applied to a set.

⚠️ **A removal that breaks the trip says so** — *"removing this leaves Wed and Fri uncovered"* — and
offers to re-solve. It never silently returns a shorter capsule. Same honesty as the shortfall screen.

---

## What this reuses (it is mostly assembly)

| Need | Already built |
|---|---|
| Destination weather + geocoding | `lib/weather/` — Open-Meteo, forecast by coordinate |
| Occasion → formality band | `lib/generator/rules.ts` — `personalBand`, `applyFormalityOverride` |
| Building and scoring outfits | `lib/generator/` — candidates, colour, score, rank |
| Naming a look and the "why" | `lib/generator/rerank.ts` |
| Persisting a set of outfits | `lib/outfits/` — the daily-drop write path generalises |
| The location picker UI | one component already serves Settings and the Stylist weather pill (#9c) |
| Gating | `lib/billing/entitlements.ts` |

⚠️ **The weather read must go through `lib/weather/planning.ts`.** The generator audit found one
defect in three places — the pipeline reading the CURRENT hour while a look is worn all day. One
`hoursFor` helper now serves temperature and rain so they cannot drift. A trip spans days, which
makes this *more* important, not less.

---

## Data model

```
trips
  id, user_id, destination_label, lat, lon, timezone,
  start_date, end_date,
  occasion_mix jsonb,        -- { work: 3, everyday: 2, evening: 2, weekend: 0 }
  rewear_level int,          -- 1–5, the meter position
  created_at

trip_items                   -- the capsule
  trip_id, item_id, pinned boolean

-- per-day looks reuse outfits/outfit_items, keyed by trip
outfits: + trip_id, + trip_day date
```

⚠️ **RLS on both new tables**, `user_id = auth.uid()`, flat and non-recursive, as everywhere else.

⚠️ **`trip_id` is nullable on `outfits`** — every existing row predates it, exactly as `thumb_url`
was on `items`. The daily drop must be untouched by this migration.

---

## Screens

Four, at 390×844. The visual design exists in the **Styling** project and is on-system — its values
were verified against `app/globals.css` and match exactly.

1. **Trip setup** — destination (the existing picker), date range, occasion mix with +/− steppers,
   the re-wear meter. One screen, not a wizard. Primary: *"Plan the trip"*.
2. **The capsule** — kicker `LISBON · 12–18 MAY`, the **number as a serif headline** ("Nine pieces."),
   a stat trio (pieces / days / outfits), the cutouts as the largest elements on screen, and the
   italic why line with the rust `J`. Primary: *"See the days"*.
3. **Day by day** — per day: date, occasion, forecast, the look as a flat-lay, **wear counts**, and
   the why. Primary: *"Save packing list"*.
4. **Shortfall** — names what is missing *and why it matters*, then offers what it **can** build
   ("A five-day capsule", `7 pieces / 5 days / 2 uncovered`).

⚠️ **Screen 4 is required, not an edge case.** This project has fixed "silently returns nothing"
three times (`personalBand`, outerwear, seasons).

### Small drift to fix when building from the comp

- Garment colours near-miss the tokens: the comp uses `#C6A374` / `#33455B`; the app has
  `--color-dna-camel: #B89A6A` and `--color-dna-navy: #2C3A4C`. Snap to the DNA swatches.
- `#3A3A3D`, `#2E2D31`, `#241D18` are invented greys — map onto the surface ramp.
- Trip setup lacks the back control the other three screens have.
- Day-by-day is the rust-heaviest screen (three `#D69873` occasion labels plus two `J` glyphs) —
  check it against the **One Rust Rule** (~10% max).

---

## Testing

- **The solve is pure and unit-tested without a database**: `capsule.ts`, `rewear.ts`, `schedule.ts`.
  Fixed wardrobes in, deterministic capsules out.
- ⚠️ **The AI is stubbed inside `rerank()`** via `FITCHECK_STUB_AI`, as the e2e suite already does —
  so the tested path is the shipped path and CI spends nothing.
- **e2e covers the journey**: setup → capsule → days, plus the shortfall state with a deliberately
  inadequate closet.
- ⚠️ **Test the pathological wardrobes**: a closet that can dress nothing, one that can dress
  everything with two items, one with no outerwear against a cold forecast. The gap card in wear-stats
  was rebuilt **three times** because it was reasoned about rather than measured against real data.

## Out of scope for v1

- Dress-code-by-destination (decision #7).
- Sharing a packing list outside the app — the share affordance in the comp is Phase 2 (`@vercel/og`).
- Multi-destination trips.
- Anything about luggage size or weight.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/1curafu/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.3.0/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

2. **Trips end to end** — migration, actions, the four screens, editing.

Editing folds into #2 rather than becoming a third plan, because if the solve takes `pinned`/`excluded` from day one, editing is nearly free.

Both delivered. Fair enough on judging the capsule method after testing — that's exactly what Task 5 is for.

## The spec

All seven decisions closed. Two are worth re-reading because they're deliberate *nos*:

- **#7** — weather yes, dress-code-by-city no, because **the occasion mix already is the dress code** and it comes from you rather than from us guessing at a city name.
- **#5** — recorded in `generation_events`, but **not limited**. Metering a Pro feature would contradict "unlimited daily looks"; recording it means you can see usage if it ever surprises you.

## Plan 1 — the capsule engine

Six tasks, all pure logic. No database, no UI, no AI — the outfit builder is injected so `lib/packing/` never imports `lib/generator/`, and Task 6 greps to prove it.

**`pinned` and `excluded` are in the signature from day one**, even though nothing uses them yet. Editing the capsule is *this same solve with constraints*, so building them in now costs nothing and avoids a rewrite.

## ⚠️ The self-review caught a real bug — in my own algorithm

I'd specified textbook greedy set-cover: *add the item covering the most uncovered days*. **That doesn't work here**, and it would have failed silently.

An outfit is **conjunctive** — a top AND a bottom AND shoes. So no single item covers any day until all three categories are present. Every candidate scores a gain of zero on the first pass, the loop exits immediately, and the capsule comes back empty.

Replaced with: walk the days in order, dress each first from pieces already chosen (free), fall back to the whole closet (which costs new pieces). Re-use is preferred **structurally** rather than by a heuristic. I traced all ten tests against it by hand — they pass, including the re-wear one that forces a third shirt at level 2 on a six-day trip.

The plan now says loudly why it isn't textbook, so nobody "simplifies" it back. And Task 4 gained a fourth negative test for exactly that regression.

## Plan 2 is deliberately not written yet

Trips end-to-end — migration, actions, four screens, editing. I've held it because **Task 5's calibration decides things Plan 2 would otherwise assume**: the floor value determines typical capsule size, and "Nine pieces." is currently a number from a mockup, not a measurement. Writing the screens plan first would bake in a guess.

Your "I'll say after testing" fits that exactly.

Want me to start executing Plan 1, or leave it until you've had a look?

gh pr create --base main --head feat/packing-capsule-engine --title "Packing: the capsule engine" --body-file - <<'MD'
Plan 1 of 2 for packing mode. **Pure logic only** — no database, no UI, no AI. The screens and persistence are plan 2, deliberately held until this one's calibration was known.

- **Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-26-packing-mode-design.md` (all seven scoping decisions closed)
- **Plan:** `docs/superpowers/plans/todo/2026-08-26-packing-capsule-engine.md`

## What it does

Picks the smallest set of closet pieces that can dress every day of a trip, with per-category re-wear limits, a quality floor, and support for pinned/excluded items.

Three modules under `lib/packing/`, with the outfit builder **injected** — so the whole thing is unit-tested without a database and never imports `lib/generator/`. Task 6 greps to prove it:

```
lib/packing/capsule.ts:1:import { maxWears } from "./rewear";
lib/packing/schedule.ts:1:import type { CapsuleResult, TripDay } from "./capsule";
```

## ⚠️ Not textbook set-cover, and the reason matters

The plan originally specified classic greedy: *add the item covering the most uncovered days*. **That cannot work here**, and it would have failed silently.

An outfit is **conjunctive** — a top AND a bottom AND shoes — so no single item covers any day until all three categories are present. Every candidate scores a gain of zero on the first pass, the loop exits, and the capsule comes back empty. Caught while reviewing the plan, before a line was written.

Instead it walks days in order, dressing each first from pieces already chosen (free), falling back to the whole closet (which costs new pieces). Re-use is preferred **structurally** rather than by a heuristic. The code says loudly why, so nobody simplifies it back.

## ⚠️ The negative pass found a tautology — in my own test

Task 4 breaks each guard and confirms the test goes red. Three of four did. **The fourth did not**, and that is the finding.

*"re-uses pieces instead of packing one outfit per day"* passed **even with re-use deliberately broken**, because the test's builder always returned the first matching item — identical output whether given the chosen subset or the whole closet. The assertion could never have failed. Same shape as the `expect(gap === null || gap.unlocks > 0)` tautology this project shipped once before.

The builder now rotates its pick by day, so given the whole closet it chooses a different top every day; only a solve that genuinely prefers what it has keeps the capsule small. A second test states it as a guarantee rather than a bound — one top for three days, not merely "fewer than nine pieces".

All four guards now go red when broken.

## Calibration — measured, not invented

`scripts/calibrate-packing-floor.ts`, run against the real 26-item closet, 7-day trip (3 work / 2 everyday / 2 evening), mild spring forecast:

| level | pieces | uncovered | worst day |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 — default | **7** | 0 | 0.850 |
| 5 — pack light | **5** | 0 | 0.850 |
| 1 — fresh every day | 12 | **3** | 0.775 |

`QUALITY_FLOOR = 0.7` — the highest value that rejects nothing this closet can legitimately build. A guard, not a filter.

**Three findings that matter more than the constant:**

1. **`scoreCombo` is barely discriminating here** — every combination lands between 0.775 and 0.850, a 0.075 spread. A floor can only ever be a backstop against something egregious, never a quality dial. No UI should imply otherwise.
2. **"Fresh every day" cannot dress a 7-day trip from 26 items** — twelve pieces and still three days uncovered, at *any* floor. The shortfall screen is reachable from an ordinary closet at an ordinary setting, which makes it load-bearing rather than defensive.
3. **The design comp's number is wrong.** It says *"Nine pieces."* Measured, this closet needs **seven** at the default. Plan 2 renders measured numbers, not the mockup's.

## Other decisions worth keeping

- **`maxWears` returns TOTAL wears, not re-wears.** The comp's labels were ambiguous ("Once" — one wear, or one repeat?). These aren't, and the comp's copy should be reconciled to them.
- **Per-category limits aren't a refinement** — a flat "wear everything twice" on a 7-day trip asks for ~4 pairs of shoes.

content.text:
**PR #48 is up and green:** https://github.com/1curafu/Fitcheck/pull/48

All six tasks done. 787 unit tests, tsc/build clean, lint at main's baseline, rebased onto `main` after you merged #47.

## The measurement — and it changes a number in your design

Run against your **real 26-item closet**, 7-day trip (3 work / 2 everyday / 2 evening):

| level | pieces | uncovered |
|---|---|---|
| 3 — default | **7** | 0 |
| 5 — pack light | **5** | 0 |
| 1 — fresh every day | 12 | **3** |

Three things fell out of that:

1. **The comp says "Nine pieces." Measured, it's seven.** The mockup number was plausible and wrong. Plan 2 renders measured numbers.
2. **"Fresh every day" can't dress a week from 26 items** — twelve pieces and *still* three days uncovered, at any floor. So the shortfall screen isn't defensive design for sparse closets; it's reachable at an ordinary setting.
3. **`scoreCombo` barely discriminates** — every combination lands between 0.775 and 0.850, a 0.075 spread. So the quality floor can only ever be a backstop against something egregious, never a quality dial. `QUALITY_FLOOR = 0.7` is recorded with the full table so nobody later mistakes it for a knob.

## Two defects the plan caught in itself

**The algorithm I originally specified could not work.** Textbook greedy set-cover adds the item covering the most days — but an outfit is *conjunctive* (top AND bottom AND shoes), so no single item covers any day until all three are present. Every candidate would gain zero, the loop would exit, and the capsule would come back empty. Caught in the plan's self-review, before any code.

**The re-use test was a tautology.** Task 4 breaks each guard and checks the test goes red — three of four did, and the fourth didn't. *"re-uses pieces"* passed **with re-use deliberately broken**, because its builder returned the first matching item either way. Same shape as the `gap === null || gap.unlocks > 0` tautology this project shipped once before. The builder now rotates its pick by day, and all four guards fail properly when broken.

That's the second time this session that the step most tempting to skip found the real problem.

## Next

**Plan 2** — trips end to end: migration, server actions, entitlement gate, `generation_events`, the four screens, and the editing UI on top of the `pinned`/`excluded` this engine already accepts.

I can write it now — and it'll use seven pieces, not nine. Or you test the capsule method first, as you said, and we adjust before the screens get built on top of it.
so wait, it doesnt work right now?

Correct — **not as a feature you can use.** Let me be precise about what exists.

**What works right now:** the engine. `solveCapsule()` is real, tested 13 ways, and I ran it against your actual 26-item closet through the calibration script — it produced a genuine 7-piece capsule covering all 7 days. The algorithm is proven on your real data, not on fixtures.

**What doesn't exist:** everything that would let you *use* it. No `/packing` route, no screens, no `trips` table, nothing in the app calls it. If you open Fitcheck right now, packing mode is still just a line in the upgrade sheet.

So it's a library, not a feature.

That was the deliberate split — and my reasoning was that the engine's calibration would tell us things the screens need to know. It did: the comp's "Nine pieces" is really seven, and the shortfall screen turns out to be reachable at an ordinary setting rather than being a rare edge case. Building the screens first would have baked in both mistakes.

But I should have been blunter that Plan 1 ships nothing user-visible. That's on me.

**Plan 2 is what makes it real:** migration (`trips`, `trip_items`, `outfits.trip_id`), the server actions that wire the engine to the generator, the entitlement gate, and the four screens — with editing on top of the `pinned`/`excluded` the engine already accepts.

Want me to write and execute it now? It's the bigger of the two, but nothing in it is uncertain any more — the risky part is already measured and merged-ready.
should i merge it or we will make 2 pr together

**Merge it.** Three reasons:

1. **Zero risk** — nothing calls it. It's pure logic with no callers, so it cannot break anything on `main`.
2. **Review quality** — Plan 2 is big on its own. Stacking the engine underneath means reviewing an algorithm and four screens in one diff.
3. **It's this repo's pattern** — #40, #41, #42–45, #46, #47 each merged separately, one per plan.

The only argument for waiting is that `main` carries unused code for a while. That's cosmetic, and if testing shows the method is wrong, a follow-up PR is easier than a branch drifting behind `main`.

## But there's a gap in the plan

You said you'd judge the capsule method after testing — **and right now you have no way to test it.** No UI, and the calibration script only prints counts (`7 pieces, 0 uncovered`). A number doesn't tell you whether it's a suitcase you'd actually pack.

That's the real question: *does a camel overcoat, two oxfords and a charcoal trouser look like a week in Lisbon, or does it look like a machine picked it?* Counts can't answer that. Garment names can.

Let me extend the script to print the actual capsule — the pieces by name, and the day-by-day assignment with wear counts. Something like:

```
level 3 · 7 pieces, 7 days

  CAPSULE
  Camel overcoat · Pale Blue Oxford · Cream Oxford · ...

  Tue 12  work      Pale Blue Oxford · Charcoal Trouser · Suede Loafer
  Wed 13  work      Cream Oxford · Charcoal Trouser (2nd) · Suede Loafer (2nd)
  ...
```

Ten minutes, read-only, and it turns "7 pieces" into something you can have an opinion about — **before** Plan 2 builds four screens on top of the method.

Merge #48, and shall I add that so you can actually evaluate it?
i will test it with ui, make all things now, so i will merge #48?

Yes — merge #48. It's green, self-contained, and nothing depends on it breaking.

I'll build Plan 2 stacked on that branch and rebase once it lands. Let me gather what I need first.

-- A trip is a real entity, not a one-shot render (spec decision #4). You plan on
-- Sunday, pack on Thursday and check it at the airport; if it were regenerated
-- each time it would answer differently every time and nobody would trust it.
-- Same shape as the daily drop (Decision 5), keyed by trip instead of by day.
create table if not exists public.trips (
  id                 uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id            uuid not null references auth.users(id) on delete cascade,
  destination_label  text not null,
  lat                double precision not null,
  lon                double precision not null,
  timezone           text not null,
  start_date         date not null,
  end_date           date not null,
  -- { "work": 3, "everyday": 2, "evening": 2, "weekend": 0 }
  occasion_mix       jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb,
  -- The re-wear meter position, 1-5. `maxWears` clamps, so one bad row degrades
  -- a trip rather than breaking it.
  rewear_level       int not null default 3,
  created_at         timestamptz not null default now()
);

create table if not exists public.trip_items (
  trip_id uuid not null references public.trips(id) on delete cascade,
  item_id uuid not null references public.items(id) on delete cascade,
  -- The user insisted on this piece: seeded into the solve at zero cost and it
  -- survives a re-solve.
  pinned  boolean not null default false,
  primary key (trip_id, item_id)
);

-- Per-day looks reuse outfits/outfit_items rather than a third table.
-- ⚠️ NULLABLE, and that is load-bearing: every existing row predates this, and
-- the daily drop must be completely untouched by this migration.
alter table public.outfits add column if not exists trip_id uuid references public.trips(id) on delete cascade;
alter table public.outfits add column if not exists trip_day date;

create index if not exists outfits_trip_idx on public.outfits (trip_id, trip_day);
create index if not exists trips_user_idx on public.trips (user_id, start_date desc);

alter table public.trips enable row level security;
alter table public.trip_items enable row level security;

create policy "trips_rw_own" on public.trips
  for all using (user_id = (select auth.uid())) with check (user_id = (select auth.uid()));

-- `trip_items` has no user_id of its own; ownership is the parent trip's. Kept
-- FLAT — one EXISTS, no recursion — per the project's RLS rule.
create policy "trip_items_rw_own" on public.trip_items
  for all using (exists (select 1 from public.trips t where t.id = trip_id and t.user_id = (select auth.uid())))
  with check (exists (select 1 from public.trips t where t.id = trip_id and t.user_id = (select auth.uid())));

-- A trip is one metered event alongside drop/regenerate/styled. RECORDED, NOT
-- LIMITED (spec decision #5): metering a Pro feature would contradict the
-- "unlimited daily looks" it is sold on, but a trip that writes nothing to the
-- ledger is invisible when someone asks what a user actually costs.
alter table public.generation_events drop constraint if exists generation_events_kind_check;
alter table public.generation_events add constraint generation_events_kind_check
  check (kind in ('drop', 'regenerate', 'styled', 'trip'));

grant select, insert, update, delete on public.trips to authenticated;
grant select, insert, update, delete on public.trip_items to authenticated;

That answers itself from the audit. The rule already in the code is: **destinations get nav; pushed detail screens and flows don't.**

| has nav | no nav |
|---|---|
| closet, generate, calendar, profile (the 4 tabs) · settings, stats, **packing** | closet/[itemId], outfits/[id], closet/upload, onboarding, **packing/[tripId]**, **packing/[tripId]/days** |

My routes follow it exactly. And I'd keep it, for a concrete reason: **the trip screens have a sticky bottom action bar** ("See the days"). Adding nav underneath means two stacked bottom bars — and `docs/STATE.md` records a real bug where `MobileNav` at `z-50` painted *over* `RefineSheet`'s primary action. Item detail, the canonical screen, has the same shape and no nav.

Accessibility isn't harmed as long as every no-nav screen has a working way back.

**Which is where your question found a real bug I'd just introduced.** My shells render `ScreenHeader` with a back button and a title — then the body replaces it with a header that has *neither*. So the back control and the title paint, then vanish. That is exactly the Profile mistake `STATE.md` warns about.

`rankTopN` already had the seam — `RECENT_WEIGHT`, documented as *"a preference, never an eliminator."*

## ⚠️ My first attempt made it worse

It took your capsule from **six pieces to seven while the days still repeated** — worse on both counts.

`rankTopN` subtracts the penalty *from the score*, and the solve compares that score against `QUALITY_FLOOR`. So a fully-repeated outfit sank below the floor, the free branch failed, and **the solve bought a piece to escape its own variety nudge.**

The fix: the preference **orders without scoring** — the winner is re-scored without the penalty before it's returned.

**The unit tests couldn't see any of this.** Their fake builders return a flat `score: 1` and never touch the floor. Only running it against your actual closet showed it. Two regression tests now cover it, both verified to go red when I revert the fix.

## After

Back to **six pieces**, and days vary where the case holds an alternative — day 5 swaps trousers, day 7 swaps to the linen oxford.

Days 1–3 still repeat, and that's correct: at that point nothing else is packed to swap to. Variety improves as the capsule fills, which is honest — the alternative would be a hidden purchase.
